lessons.title: Wi-Fi generations and multi-user features
lessons.summary: Compare streams, channel width, modulation and scheduling as different improvements.
lessons.body:
Switched Ethernet commonly gives each device a dedicated wired link. Wi-Fi stations share radio resources, but not every station can hear every other. Modern multi-user techniques allow coordinated simultaneous transmissions, and spatial reuse can allow concurrent transmissions in different coverage areas. Radio conditions change with interference, motion and obstacles.

Almost everything distinctive about Wi-Fi follows from that shared, changeable medium: how devices take turns, why they cannot detect collisions, how a slow active client can consume airtime needed by another client, and why a product’s aggregate advertised PHY rates do not predict one client’s application throughput.

## The 802.11 generations

Wi-Fi is the Wi-Fi Alliance's brand for the IEEE **802.11** standards. In 2018 the Alliance introduced generation numbers so people did not need to remember letters.

| Name | Standard | Bands | Key additions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legacy | 802.11b/a/g | b/g: 2.4; a: 5 GHz | b up to 11 Mbit/s; a/g up to 54, with OFDM for a/g |
| Wi-Fi 4 | 802.11n (2009) | 2.4, 5 GHz | MIMO, 40 MHz, frame aggregation |
| Wi-Fi 5 | 802.11ac (2013) | 5 GHz | 80/160 MHz, 256-QAM, DL MU-MIMO |
| Wi-Fi 6 | 802.11ax; certification began 2019 | 2.4, 5 GHz | OFDMA, 1024-QAM, TWT |
| Wi-Fi 6E | 802.11ax | adds 6 GHz | additional spectrum, subject to local rules |
| Wi-Fi 7 | 802.11be; certification began 2024 | 2.4, 5, 6 GHz | 320 MHz, 4096-QAM, MLO |

Dates move: Wi-Fi Alliance certification for Wi-Fi 7 began in January 2024, before IEEE approved 802.11be (September 2024) and published it (July 2025). The next amendment, **802.11bn** ("Ultra High Reliability"), was still a draft in October 2026, with IEEE's own timeline estimating approval in 2028. Check the IEEE 802.11 timeline page for current status.

What each change buys:

- **MIMO** (multiple-input multiple-output): several antennas send independent **spatial streams** on the same frequency at once. Two streams roughly double the rate. The usable count depends on both endpoints and the radio channel; antenna count alone does not establish it.
- **Wider channels**: rate scales roughly with width, so 80 MHz carries about four times a 20 MHz channel.
- **Denser modulation (QAM)**: 256-QAM carries 8 bits per symbol, 1024-QAM 10, 4096-QAM 12. Each step needs a much cleaner signal, so achievable modulation depends on signal quality, interference and hardware, not a fixed distance boundary.
- **OFDMA** (Wi-Fi 6): the channel is split into **resource units**, so the AP can send to or receive from several clients in one transmission instead of one at a time. This can reduce per-client access overhead, depending on scheduling, compatible clients and workload.
- **Target Wake Time** (Wi-Fi 6): devices negotiate when to wake, saving battery for phones and IoT sensors.
- **6 GHz** (Wi-Fi 6E and 7): additional spectrum for capable devices, subject to national power, indoor/outdoor and coexistence rules. It is not interference-free. Country allocations change: for example, in July 2026 Ofcom decided to extend UK licence-exempt Wi-Fi from 5925–6425 MHz up to 6585 MHz, allowing Wi-Fi in the rest of the upper band only under database-controlled coordination, so an undated “UK has only 500 MHz” statement is out of date.
- **Multi-Link Operation** (Wi-Fi 7): coordinates multiple links; concurrent transmission/reception depends on the MLO mode and hardware. It does not require every device to transmit on three bands simultaneously.

## Key takeaways
- Compare streams, channel width, modulation and scheduling as different improvements.
- A generation label does not establish supported modes, spectrum permission or measured throughput.

lessons.title: Modulation, signal quality and capacity
lessons.summary: More constellation points add bits logarithmically and need cleaner signals.
lessons.body:
Each new Wi-Fi generation advertises a denser modulation: 256-QAM, then 1024-QAM, then 4096-QAM. The gain per step is smaller than the numbers suggest, and only clients with a very clean signal can use it.

## Why denser modulation needs a cleaner signal

A QAM symbol is one of a fixed number of possible points (amplitude-and-phase combinations). The receiver measures the incoming wave and decides which point was sent. The number of bits one symbol carries grows with the logarithm of the number of points:

```formula essential
b = log_2(M)
where
b: the number of bits carried by one QAM symbol on one subcarrier
M: the number of distinct points in the QAM constellation, e.g. 256, 1024 or 4096
log_2: the base-2 logarithm: the power you must raise 2 to in order to get the number, so log_2(1024) = 10 because 2^10 = 1024
In words: every doubling of the number of constellation points adds just one bit per symbol.
```

So 256-QAM carries 8 bits, 1024-QAM 10 bits and 4096-QAM 12 bits. Going from 1024 to 4096 points adds only 2 bits (+20%), but squeezes four times as many points into the same space, so neighbouring points sit much closer together. Noise that a 256-QAM receiver shrugs off makes a 4096-QAM receiver pick the wrong point.

That is why **rate adaptation** matters: a client near the access point with little interference may use the densest modulation, while one further away or behind walls drops to a sparser, more robust one. Achievable modulation depends on signal quality, interference and hardware, not a fixed distance boundary.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Reading a finely marked dial through fogged glasses
> A dial marked in tenths tells you more per glance than one marked in halves. But if your glasses are fogged, the fine marks blur together and you misread them, while the coarse marks are still easy.
>
> **How it maps:** Each mark is a constellation point and one glance is one symbol. More marks carry more information per glance (more bits per symbol), but only when the view is clear (high signal-to-noise ratio). Fog is noise and interference; switching to a coarser dial is rate adaptation choosing a lower-order modulation.
>
> **Where it stops:** QAM points are spread over two dimensions (amplitude and phase), not along one scale. Errors are probabilistic, and error-correcting codes repair some misreadings, so a radio does not simply fail at one fog level.

## The ceiling: Shannon capacity

The networks foundations module introduced the **Shannon–Hartley theorem**: for a channel disturbed by random (Gaussian) noise, no modulation or coding can reliably exceed a capacity set by bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

```formula reference
C = B log_2(1 + (S / N))
where
C: the channel capacity: the highest reliable data rate theoretically possible, in bits per second (bit/s)
B: the channel bandwidth, in hertz (Hz)
S: the received signal power, in watts (W)
N: the noise power in the same channel, in watts (W)
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
In words: capacity grows in proportion to channel width but only with the logarithm of signal quality, so doubling the channel width roughly doubles the ceiling while doubling signal power adds much less once the signal is already well above the noise.
```

For example, a 20 MHz channel at 30 dB SNR (signal 1000 times the noise power) has a theoretical ceiling of about 200 Mbit/s, roughly 10 bits per second per hertz. SNR is quoted in decibels: every extra 10 dB means ten times the power ratio.

The ceiling is not a minimum-SNR specification for 1024-QAM. Coding, error targets, interference and hardware determine a real radio's requirements. Real radios also lose rate to coding and guard intervals, so the rates in the PHY-rate lesson sit below this bound. The practical lesson: wider channels and more spatial streams add capacity roughly in proportion, while denser modulation adds only a little and only where the signal is clean.

## Key takeaways
- More constellation points add bits logarithmically and need cleaner signals.
- Rate adaptation picks the densest modulation the current signal quality supports.
- The Gaussian-noise capacity model is a theoretical bound, not a radio throughput measurement.

## Further reading
- [Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (original paper)](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)
- [Quadrature amplitude modulation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrature_amplitude_modulation)

questions.prompt: An access point is upgraded from 1024-QAM to 4096-QAM support. Clients range from a laptop on the same desk to phones three rooms away. Which prediction is most accurate?

options.text: Every client gets about four times the throughput, because the constellation has four times as many points
options.explanation: Bits per symbol grow with the base-2 logarithm of the number of points, so four times the points adds only two bits (10 to 12). Distant clients may not be able to use 4096-QAM at all.

options.text: Only clients with a very clean signal gain, and then by about 20% at most in raw rate; distant clients see little or no change
options.explanation: Correct. 4096-QAM carries 12 bits per symbol against 10 for 1024-QAM. Its points sit much closer together, so only high-SNR clients can decode it; rate adaptation keeps the others on sparser modulation.

options.text: Distant clients gain the most, because denser modulation compensates for a weak signal
options.explanation: The opposite: denser constellations need a cleaner signal. Weak-signal clients fall back to more robust, lower-order modulation.

options.text: No client gains, because Shannon capacity is fixed by the channel width alone
options.explanation: Shannon capacity depends on both bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio. A clean, nearby link can have headroom that denser modulation can use.

questions.workedExample:
1. Bits per symbol grow with the logarithm of the number of constellation points: 1024 points give 10 bits, 4096 points give 12. Quadrupling the points adds two bits, about 20% more raw rate before coding and overhead.
2. Packing four times as many points into the same space puts neighbouring points much closer together, so a receiver needs a much cleaner signal to tell them apart.
3. Rate adaptation therefore uses 4096-QAM only on links with high signal-to-noise ratio, typically a client close to the AP with little interference.
4. Clients further away keep using sparser modulation, so the upgrade changes little for them. It is a modest top-end gain, not a fourfold improvement.

lessons.title: Wi-Fi contention, backoff and acknowledgments
lessons.summary: Count down backoff only while the channel is idle; failure grows the contention window up to its cap.
lessons.body:
Wi-Fi stations on one channel share the air with no referee deciding who speaks next in the basic access mode. They take turns by listening, waiting a random time and treating a missing acknowledgment as failure. This explains why a busy channel gets slower and less predictable as more devices compete.

## Sharing the air: CSMA/CA

Classic shared Ethernet used **CSMA/CD**: listen before sending, and if you *detect a collision* while transmitting, stop, jam and back off. Wi-Fi cannot do the "CD" part:

1. Ordinary Wi-Fi radios do not implement Ethernet-style collision detection while sending; their own transmit signal makes simultaneous sensing of weak incoming signals difficult.
2. A collision may happen at the receiver but not be audible at the sender at all (covered in the next lesson).

So Wi-Fi tries to **avoid** collisions instead, and uses missing expected acknowledgments as an indication of failure; not every frame is individually acknowledged. The following is a simplified **DCF** contention example for acknowledged unicast using 5 GHz OFDM timings. Modern QoS traffic commonly uses EDCA with access-category parameters; broadcast/multicast and scheduled multi-user exchanges differ:

1. **Carrier sense.** Listen. If the channel is busy, wait until it goes idle.
2. **Wait DIFS.** After the channel goes idle, wait a fixed gap (34 µs on 5 GHz).
3. **Random backoff.** Pick a random whole-number count between zero and the current contention window, inclusive (9 µs slots; the window starts at 15). Count down only while the channel stays idle; freeze the counter if someone else starts sending.
4. **Transmit** when the counter hits zero.
5. **ACK.** The receiver replies after a shorter gap, SIFS (16 µs). The shorter gap gives priority over compliant contenders that sense this exchange; interference and hidden terminals can still corrupt the ACK.
6. **No ACK?** Assume a collision or corruption, grow the contention window (here 15, 31, 63 ... up to 1023) and try again. After a retry limit, drop the frame.

```
busy |DIFS| backoff |  DATA  |SIFS|ACK|
-----+----+---------+--------+----+---+
      34us  k x 9us           16us
```

In the timeline, k is the random number of slots the station drew.

DIFS is SIFS plus two slots (16 + 2 × 9 = 34 µs). That difference is the whole point: a receiver about to send an ACK only has to wait 16 µs, so it starts before any compliant contender that is waiting for 34 µs of silence.

## Why the window doubles

The contention window roughly doubles after each failure, up to a cap:

```formula reference
CW_new = min(2(CW_old + 1) − 1, CW_max)
where
CW_new: the contention window for the next attempt, in slots
CW_old: the contention window before the failed attempt, in slots; 15 for a first attempt in this example
CW_max: the cap on the contention window, 1023 slots here
min: the minimum function: whichever of its values is smaller
In words: every failed attempt roughly doubles the range of random waits a station chooses from, until the range reaches its cap.
```

If two stations both wait for a busy channel to end and then send immediately, they collide. The random countdown spreads them out. When failures keep happening, the channel is probably crowded, so each failing station widens its range and backs off harder. After three failures in this example, the station draws from 0 to 127 slots, up to about 1.1 ms of counted idle time, before busy periods and interframe gaps are added.

The consequences for performance follow directly:

- **More stations, more waiting.** Each extra contender adds collisions and frozen countdowns, so per-station throughput falls and delay becomes more variable.
- **Retries cost airtime.** A failed transmission still occupied the air, and the retry waits longer.
- **Latency spikes.** A frame that fails several times can wait milliseconds before it is finally sent or dropped.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A group conversation with no chairperson
> In a group with no chair, people wait for a pause, then hesitate for a moment before speaking. If two start at once, both stop, and next time each waits a little longer before trying again.
>
> **How it maps:** Waiting for a pause is carrier sense and DIFS; the brief random hesitation is the backoff count; both stopping and waiting longer next time is the contention window doubling after a missing ACK. The person who was asked a question answers straight away, which is the short SIFS gap before the ACK.
>
> **Where it stops:** People in a room notice when they talk over each other. A Wi-Fi sender usually cannot: it only learns of failure when the expected ACK does not arrive, and some stations cannot hear each other at all.

There is also **virtual carrier sense**: eligible frames carry Duration/ID information that can reserve remaining exchange time. Stations update their **NAV** (network allocation vector) according to protocol rules. Some fields are zero or have other meanings; physical carrier sensing still applies.

## Key takeaways
- Count down backoff only while the channel is idle; failure grows the contention window up to its cap.
- SIFS gives immediate replies priority over ordinary DCF contention under the stated sensing assumptions.
- More contenders mean more collisions, longer backoffs and more variable delay.

## Further reading
- [Carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrier-sense_multiple_access_with_collision_avoidance)
- [ns-3 Wi-Fi model: DCF, EDCA and protection mechanisms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nsnam/ns-3-dev-git/master/src/wifi/doc/source/wifi-design.rst)

questions.prompt: Why does ordinary Wi-Fi contention use collision avoidance rather than Ethernet-style detection of collisions during a transmission?

options.text: Wi-Fi frames are encrypted, so a radio cannot tell its own frame from a collision
options.explanation: Encryption protects the payload; it has nothing to do with sensing energy on the channel. Collision detection is a physical-layer problem, not a security one.

options.text: Its own transmission is vastly stronger at its antenna than any distant signal, so it cannot hear a collision while sending, and the collision may only happen at the receiver anyway
options.explanation: Correct. A transmitting radio is effectively deafened by itself, and with hidden terminals the collision happens at the receiver where the sender could never hear it. So Wi-Fi avoids collisions and infers failure from a missing ACK.

options.text: Radio waves travel too slowly for collisions to be detected in time
options.explanation: Radio travels at nearly the speed of light, faster than signals in copper. Propagation speed is not the obstacle.

options.text: 802.11 uses full-duplex radios, so collisions never happen
options.explanation: Wi-Fi is half duplex: a station sends or receives on a channel, not both. Collisions certainly happen, which is why exponential backoff exists.

questions.workedExample: The transmitting radio’s own signal makes sensing weak concurrent incoming signals difficult. More fundamentally, interference depends on what arrives at the receiver: hidden senders may not hear one another. Ordinary Wi-Fi uses carrier sensing, contention and missing expected ACKs instead of Ethernet-style collision detection. No fixed power ratio or claim about every possible radio design is needed.

questions.prompt: In the simplified DCF model, a station on a crowded channel has three transmissions in a row fail with no ACK. The retry limit still allows another attempt. What happens to its next attempt, and what does that mean for the user?

options.text: It retries immediately, so a failed frame costs almost no extra time
options.explanation: Retrying at once would just collide again with the other contenders. DCF draws a new random backoff from a larger window after each failure.

options.text: Its contention window resets to the starting value, so the retry is no slower than a fresh frame
options.explanation: The window resets after a success (or after the frame is dropped), not after a failure. Each failure widens the window.

options.text: It draws its backoff from a window roughly twice the previous one, so the expected wait grows and delay becomes larger and more variable
options.explanation: Correct. The window goes 15, 31, 63, then 127 slots in this example. Spreading retries more widely reduces repeat collisions but adds waiting, so loaded Wi-Fi shows longer and jumpier delay.

options.text: Every other station on the channel also doubles its window, so the channel becomes quiet
options.explanation: Only the station whose own transmission failed widens its window. Other stations follow their own retry state.

questions.workedExample:
1. No ACK is taken as a sign of collision or corruption, so the station must try again.
2. Each failure roughly doubles its contention window: 15 → 31 → 63 → 127 slots after three failures in this example, capped at 1023.
3. It draws a random count from 0 up to that window and counts down only while the channel is idle, freezing while others transmit.
4. A wider range means a longer expected wait, so this frame is delayed further. Across a crowded channel this shows up as falling throughput and latency spikes.
5. If the retry limit is reached the frame is dropped; after a success the window returns to its starting value.

link.title: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance — Wikipedia

questions.prompt: In the lesson’s 5 GHz OFDM DCF example, why is SIFS (16 µs) shorter than DIFS (34 µs) for an acknowledged unicast exchange?

options.text: SIFS is shorter so that ACKs use less battery
options.explanation: Battery has nothing to do with it; the gap length is about priority on the channel.

options.text: It gives the immediate ACK priority over compliant DCF contenders that sense the exchange
options.explanation: Correct. The ACK can begin before their DIFS expires. Hidden terminals or interference can still disrupt it; this is priority, not an absolute collision-free guarantee.

options.text: SIFS allows the receiver time to decrypt the frame before acknowledging
options.explanation: SIFS includes turnaround/processing constraints, but the comparison with DIFS establishes access priority. It is not a guarantee that all security processing completes before ACK transmission.

options.text: DIFS is only used on 2.4 GHz; on 5 GHz everyone uses SIFS
options.explanation: The specified 5 GHz OFDM DCF model uses both gaps. Other PHYs and QoS access categories have their own timing parameters; contenders do not all use SIFS.

questions.workedExample:
1. In this 5 GHz OFDM DCF example, SIFS is 16 µs and DIFS is SIFS plus two 9 µs slots, 34 µs.
2. A receiver that has just received a frame carrying data starts its ACK after only 16 µs of idle time.
3. A compliant contender that sensed that frame needs 34 µs of idle time before it may even begin its backoff, so the ACK is already on the air.
4. This gives the immediate reply priority under those sensing conditions. It is not an absolute guarantee: hidden senders and interference can still corrupt the ACK, and other PHYs and EDCA categories use different parameters.

lessons.title: Hidden and exposed terminals
lessons.summary: A hidden sender can interfere at a receiver it cannot hear directly.
lessons.body:
Carrier sense assumes that if the channel sounds quiet to you, it is quiet at your receiver. Two failure patterns break that assumption in opposite directions: a sender you cannot hear (hidden) and a sender you can hear but need not wait for (exposed).

## The hidden terminal problem and RTS/CTS

Carrier sense only works if every station can hear every other. Often they cannot.

```
  (A) ~~~~~~ [AP] ~~~~~~ (C)
   A hears AP, C hears AP,
   A and C cannot hear each other
```

A and C both sense an idle channel and transmit at once. Their frames can interfere **at the AP**, causing missing ACKs and retries. Capture effects or different timings can allow some frames to succeed; throughput need not collapse in every such topology.

**RTS/CTS** can mitigate this when the relevant contenders receive the protection frames:

1. A sends a short **Request To Send** to the AP, with the duration of the exchange.
2. The AP replies **Clear To Send**, carrying the remaining protected exchange time.
3. C cannot hear A's RTS, but it *can* hear the AP's CTS, so it sets its NAV and stays quiet.
4. A sends its data; the AP ACKs.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Two people either side of a hedge
> Alice and Carol stand on opposite sides of a tall hedge, each talking to Bob, who stands in a gap in the middle. Neither can hear the other, so both start talking at once and Bob hears a jumble. The fix is for Alice to ask "Bob, may I talk for ten seconds?" and for Bob to answer aloud "Go ahead, Alice, ten seconds". Carol cannot hear Alice's question, but she hears Bob's answer and waits.
>
> **How it maps:** Alice and Carol are the hidden stations A and C, Bob is the AP, and the jumble is a collision at the receiver that neither sender can hear. Alice's question is the RTS, Bob's answer is the CTS, and Carol waiting for the stated time is setting her NAV.
>
> **Where it stops:** Bob could call out that he heard a jumble; an access point sends no such warning, so Wi-Fi senders only infer a collision from a missing ACK. A station that misses the CTS, or interference from a non-Wi-Fi source, still causes losses, and the exchange costs extra airtime on every protected transmission.

This reduces the chance of wasting a long data transmission on a hidden-terminal collision. Missed CTS frames, other interferers and overlapping reservations still permit data/ACK loss. The cost is two extra frames and gaps per exchange, so implementations can select protection using an **RTS threshold** and other policies; defaults are device-specific. Wi-Fi 6 also uses RTS/CTS-style protection automatically in some situations, such as before multi-user transmissions.

The mirror image is the **exposed terminal**: a station that hears a nearby transmission and defers, even though its own transmission would not have interfered at its intended receiver. RTS/CTS does not fix this; it is one reason dense networks waste airtime.

## Key takeaways
- A hidden sender can interfere at a receiver it cannot hear directly.
- Received RTS/CTS protection can mitigate hidden-terminal collisions; it does not solve exposed-terminal deferral.

## Further reading
- [Hidden node problem — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_node_problem)

questions.prompt: A laptop (A) on one side of a warehouse and a scanner (C) on the other can both reach the AP in the middle, but not each other. Throughput collapses whenever both are busy. What is the standard 802.11 mechanism designed for this?

options.text: Increasing the DIFS gap on both stations
options.explanation: A longer common interframe wait does not reveal hidden transmissions or reserve the receiver; it does not directly solve the stated hidden-terminal problem.

options.text: RTS/CTS: the AP's Clear To Send is heard by both, so the other station sets its NAV and stays quiet
options.explanation: Correct. This is the hidden terminal problem. A and C cannot hear each other's RTS, but both hear the AP's CTS, which carries the duration of the exchange.

options.text: Switching both stations to CSMA/CD
options.explanation: Radios cannot detect collisions while transmitting, and in any case the collision happens at the AP, where neither sender can hear it.

options.text: Using a 40 MHz channel so there is room for both
options.explanation: Increasing channel width alone does not solve hidden-terminal contention. Coordinated multi-user mechanisms are separate from simply selecting a wider channel.

questions.workedExample: A and C can interfere at the AP without sensing one another. If C successfully receives and obeys the AP’s CTS, it defers for the protected interval while A sends. RTS/CTS can reduce wasted long-frame transmissions; missing protection frames, other interference and overlapping exchanges can still cause loss.

questions.prompt: In a simplified same-channel topology, B sends to A while C wants to send to D. Assume concurrent data transmissions would not interfere at either receiver. C nevertheless senses B and defers. What is this effect, and does basic RTS/CTS automatically authorise C to ignore the busy medium?

options.text: The hidden terminal problem; RTS/CTS fixes it
options.explanation: Hidden terminals are stations that *cannot* hear each other and collide. Here C *can* hear B and defers unnecessarily: the opposite problem.

options.text: Exposed-terminal deferral; basic RTS/CTS does not automatically authorise concurrent transmission
options.explanation: Correct. Deferral can suppress a potentially useful transmission, but basic protection is not a general spatial-reuse permission system.

options.text: The performance anomaly; airtime fairness fixes it
options.explanation: The performance anomaly is about slow clients consuming airtime, not about unnecessary deferral due to overheard transmissions.

options.text: Adjacent-channel interference; moving to channel 6 fixes it
options.explanation: All four stations are on the same channel here, and C defers because it decodes B. That is co-channel deferral, not adjacent-channel noise.

questions.workedExample: The question supplies non-interference at both data receivers; merely saying D cannot hear B would not establish that C cannot harm A. C still defers because it senses the medium. This is exposed-terminal deferral. ACK interference and protocol timing also matter, so basic RTS/CTS does not automatically prove a concurrent complete exchange is safe.

lessons.title: Channels, interference and radio propagation
lessons.summary: Start with a permitted, surveyed channel plan; overlapping energy and coordinated co-channel sharing differ.
lessons.body:
Which channel an access point uses, and how wide it is, decides who it competes with and who merely interferes with it. A good channel plan is the cheapest Wi-Fi performance fix, and radio propagation explains why the bands behave differently.

## Channels and interference

**2.4 GHz** has channels only 5 MHz apart, but each transmission is about 20 MHz wide. Neighbouring channels therefore overlap, and **1, 6 and 11** is a conventional conservative 20 MHz plan where those channels are permitted. Available channels, PHY spectral masks and interference determine other viable plans; this is not the only possible set worldwide.

Channel 1 is centred at 2412 MHz and each channel number adds 5 MHz (channels 1 to 13; Japan's channel 14 is a special case). So channels 1, 6 and 11 sit at 2412, 2437 and 2462 MHz: 25 MHz apart, more than one 20 MHz-wide transmission.

Channels 1 and 3, by contrast, are only 10 MHz apart, so their 20 MHz-wide signals overlap by about half.

```
ch  1     6     11
  [====][====][====]
     [====]
    ch 3 overlaps both 1 and 6
```

Two kinds of interference behave very differently:

- **Co-channel**: your neighbour's AP is also on channel 6. When networks can sense each other, contention helps them share airtime. Collisions, hidden terminals and decoding failures can still occur.
- **Adjacent-channel**: your neighbour is on channel 3. Overlapping energy may interfere without successful frame decoding. Energy detection can still cause deferral, depending on thresholds. The result depends on power, frequency separation, placement and equipment; it is not a universal ranking of channel plans.

> [!tip] Rule of thumb
> In a dense deployment using channels 1–11, 20 MHz with a coordinated 1/6/11 plan is a useful starting point. Check the regulatory domain and survey neighbouring use; wider channels reduce the number of separate channels available.

**5 GHz** has many more 20 MHz channels, enough for several 80 MHz channels. Some are **DFS** channels shared with radar: an AP must listen for radar before using them and vacate if it detects any, which can cause a sudden channel change.

**6 GHz** excludes older 2.4/5-GHz-only Wi-Fi clients, but compatible clients can still use low rates or consume substantial airtime. Other authorised services and neighbouring networks may share spectrum.

With antennas of fixed gain, such as the small antennas in typical clients and APs, higher frequencies lose more signal over the same distance. **Free-space path loss** is the loss between two ideal antennas with nothing in the way, so it is a best case:

```formula reference
L_fs = 20 log_10((4πdf) / c)
where
L_fs: the free-space path loss between two isotropic antennas, in decibels (dB)
d: the distance between the antennas, in metres (m)
f: the signal frequency, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of light, about 299,792,458 metres per second (m/s)
π: pi, about 3.14159
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibel; every 10 dB is a factor of ten in power
In words: free-space loss rises by about 6 dB, a quarter of the received power, every time the distance or the frequency doubles.
```

At 10 m, for example, a 5.5 GHz signal arrives about 7 dB weaker than a 2.4 GHz one, roughly a fifth of the power, before any walls. Wall losses depend on material, construction, angle and frequency, and the free-space model does not predict them. Actual coverage also depends on permitted power, antenna patterns, bandwidth and receiver sensitivity; a frequency label alone does not establish range or throughput. Other things share 2.4 GHz too: Bluetooth, microwave ovens and baby monitors.

The practical consequence: as a client moves away, its signal-to-noise ratio falls, rate adaptation picks slower modulation, and each frame takes longer on air. That is why throughput falls with distance well before the connection drops, and why 5 and 6 GHz cells are usually smaller than 2.4 GHz ones.

## Key takeaways
- Start with a permitted, surveyed channel plan; overlapping energy and coordinated co-channel sharing differ.
- Free-space path loss compares frequencies under fixed gains and distance, not arbitrary indoor coverage.

## Further reading
- [List of WLAN channels — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_WLAN_channels)
- [Ofcom: 6 GHz spectrum sharing decisions](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/spectrum/innovative-use-of-spectrum/consultation-expanding-access-to-the-6-ghz-band-for-commercial-mobile-and-wi-fi-services)

questions.prompt: For three nearby 2.4 GHz APs restricted to channels 1–11 at 20 MHz width, which listed conventional channel plan avoids adjacent-channel overlap?

options.text: 1, 2 and 3
options.explanation: Adjacent 2.4 GHz channels are only 5 MHz apart, but each transmission is about 20 MHz wide, so 1, 2 and 3 overlap almost completely.

options.text: 1, 4 and 8
options.explanation: The 1-to-4 centre spacing is only 15 MHz. The conventional 1/6/11 plan provides 25 MHz between centres; exact interference also depends on spectral masks and equipment.
Correct among these choices. Centres at 2412, 2437 and 2462 MHz are 25 MHz apart. This is not a claim that no other valid plan exists worldwide.

2. Each transmission is about 20 MHz wide, so two channels need their centres more than about 20 MHz apart to avoid overlapping.

Moving the neighbour to overlapping channel 2 or 3 instead causes substantial retries without useful coordination. Given these observed conditions and choices, which channel should the neighbour use?

lessons.title: PHY rates and the number on the box
lessons.summary: An aggregate router label sums separate radios, while a single-link client uses one link at a time.
lessons.body:
A router box says "AX3000", yet a phone in the next room measures a few hundred megabits per second. Nothing is broken: the box number is a different quantity from what one client can achieve, and seeing what goes into it explains the gap.

## What the number on the box is

The number on the box is the **maximum PHY rate**, often summed across bands. A PHY rate is the raw bit rate of one link while it is transmitting: bits per symbol, times the number of subcarriers carrying data, times the number of spatial streams, divided by how long each symbol lasts.

```formula reference
R = (N_ss N_sd b r) / T_sym
where
R: the PHY rate, in megabits per second (Mbit/s)
N_ss: the number of spatial streams, e.g. 2
N_sd: the number of data subcarriers in the channel: 234 at 20 MHz, 468 at 40 MHz, 980 at 80 MHz and 1960 at 160 MHz for Wi-Fi 6
b: bits per subcarrier per symbol, set by the modulation: 1 for BPSK, 6 for 64-QAM, 8 for 256-QAM, 10 for 1024-QAM
r: the coding rate: the fraction of transmitted bits that are real data rather than error-correction redundancy, e.g. 5/6
T_sym: the duration of one OFDM symbol including its guard interval, in microseconds (µs): 12.8 µs + 0.8 µs = 13.6 µs for Wi-Fi 6 (HE) with the shortest guard interval
In words: the rate grows with more spatial streams, a wider channel (more subcarriers), denser modulation and less error-correction redundancy, and falls if each symbol takes longer.
```

An "AX3000" Wi-Fi 6 router typically gets its name like this, assuming 1024-QAM with rate-5/6 coding and a 0.8 µs guard interval on both radios:

- the 5 GHz radio, 2 streams on a 160 MHz channel: about 2,402 Mbit/s;
- the 2.4 GHz radio, 2 streams on a 40 MHz channel: about 574 Mbit/s;
- added together: about 3,000.

A conventional single-link client uses only one of those radios at a time, so it can never see the sum. Multiple-radio devices and other link-bonding arrangements existed before Wi-Fi 7; MLO standardises coordinated multi-link operation.

## Why one client gets far less

**1. The client's link rate is lower.** Many clients cannot use, or are not offered, a 160 MHz channel, and few have a clean enough signal for 1024-QAM. **Rate adaptation** picks the modulation and coding (the **MCS**) from link feedback. For one stream on an 80 MHz Wi-Fi 6 channel with a 0.8 µs guard interval, the PHY rates are approximately:

| MCS | Modulation | 1 stream, 80 MHz |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | BPSK 1/2 | 36 Mbit/s |
| 7 | 64-QAM 5/6 | 360 Mbit/s |
| 9 | 256-QAM 5/6 | 480 Mbit/s |
| 11 | 1024-QAM 5/6 | 600 Mbit/s |

A two-stream phone at MCS 7 on 80 MHz therefore runs at about 720 Mbit/s, under a third of the box figure, before any overhead. Moving further away or behind walls pushes the MCS lower still.

**2. PHY rate is not throughput.** The PHY rate excludes channel-contention waits, interframe gaps, PHY preamble airtime, MAC acknowledgments, headers and retransmissions. Ordinary single-link uploads and downloads also share the same airtime, including TCP acknowledgments, and other active stations take their turns too. The next two lessons look at fixed per-access overhead and at sharing airtime.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: The top speed in the car brochure
> A brochure quotes a car's top speed; a family that owns two cars might even add both top speeds together. Your actual journey time depends on which car you took, the road you are on, junctions, traffic lights and other traffic.
>
> **How it maps:** Each car's top speed is one radio's best-case PHY rate, and adding the two cars is the "AX3000" sum. The road conditions that keep you below top speed are the lower MCS chosen for your signal quality, and the junctions and traffic are contention, overhead and other stations sharing the air.
>
> **Where it stops:** A car can hold a steady speed between junctions; rate adaptation can change a Wi-Fi link's rate from one frame to the next, and every station on the channel takes turns on the same "road" rather than driving side by side.

## Key takeaways
- An aggregate router label sums separate radios, while a single-link client uses one link at a time.
- A client's PHY rate depends on its streams, channel width and the MCS its signal supports; overhead and sharing reduce throughput further.

## Further reading
- [Cisco: Wi-Fi throughput validation and PHY-rate tables](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/wireless-mobility/wireless-lan-wlan/212892-802-11ac-wireless-throughput-testing-and.html)

questions.prompt: An example AX3000 product label sums approximately 2,402 and 574 Mbit/s from two radios. A single-link, two-stream Wi-Fi 6 client achieves much less application throughput. Which factors can contribute? Select all that apply.

options.text: The label adds different radios’ maximum PHY rates, while this connection uses one link
options.explanation: Correct. The product aggregate is not the single-link application rate; multi-radio arrangements should not be ruled out merely by generation.

options.text: The phone negotiates a lower MCS (and perhaps 80 MHz rather than 160 MHz) because of distance and walls
options.explanation: Correct. For example, MCS 7 with two streams, 80 MHz and 0.8 µs GI gives roughly 720.6 Mbit/s PHY rate; obstacles alone do not determine this value.

options.text: Per-transmission MAC overhead, half duplex (TCP ACKs share the air) and other stations' airtime
options.explanation: Correct. Protocol overhead, radio-resource sharing and retransmissions affect goodput. There is no universal 50–70% ratio.

options.text: Wi-Fi spends time sending jam signals after every detected collision
options.explanation: Jam signals are CSMA/CD, from wired Ethernet. Wi-Fi cannot detect collisions and never sends jam signals.

options.text: TCP cannot use a window larger than 64 KB, which caps throughput at about 400 Mbit/s
options.explanation: TCP window scaling allows windows far beyond 64 KB, and in any case a 64 KB cap at a few ms RTT would give a different figure. It is not the reason.

questions.workedExample:
Follow the chain from the box to the application:

1. **The label sums two radios.** About 2,402 Mbit/s (5 GHz, 160 MHz, two streams, 1024-QAM) plus about 574 Mbit/s (2.4 GHz) is printed as "3000". A single-link client uses one radio.
2. **The client's own link is slower.** Halving the channel to 80 MHz halves the rate to about 1,201 Mbit/s; a weaker signal that only supports MCS 7 (64-QAM, rate 5/6) brings two streams down to about 720 Mbit/s.
3. **Overhead and sharing.** Contention, preambles, acknowledgments, retransmissions, TCP ACKs on the same half-duplex air and other stations' turns all reduce goodput further. There is no fixed multiplier such as 0.6.

Ethernet jam signals do not exist in Wi-Fi, and TCP window scaling removes any universal 64 KB limit, so options D and E do not explain the gap.

lessons.title: Frame aggregation and airtime efficiency
lessons.summary: A fixed channel-access cost overwhelms a short frame but can be shared by an aggregate.
lessons.body:
Every time a Wi-Fi station wins the channel it pays a fixed cost in airtime before and after its data. At high PHY rates the data itself is so quick to send that this fixed cost dominates, which is why faster modulation alone stops helping and why Wi-Fi bundles frames together.

## The fixed cost of each channel access

Each access pays for DIFS, the average backoff, the PHY preamble, SIFS and the acknowledgment. For this lesson's illustration, assume about 200 µs per access and ignore smaller per-frame costs such as delimiters and padding. This is a teaching value, not a universal measured overhead.

At 720 Mbit/s, one 1,500-byte frame takes only about 17 µs to send. So a single frame per access spends about 17 µs on data and 200 µs on overhead: only about 8% of the airtime carries data.

The share of airtime carrying data is the **airtime efficiency**:

```formula reference
η = T_data / (T_data + T_oh)
where
η: eta, the airtime efficiency: the fraction of airtime carrying data, between 0 and 1
T_data: the airtime spent sending data in one channel access, in microseconds (µs)
T_oh: the fixed overhead per channel access, in microseconds (µs)
µs: microsecond, one millionth of a second
In words: efficiency is the data time divided by the whole time of an access; a large fixed overhead makes it small unless each access carries a lot of data.
```

Two ways to raise efficiency behave very differently:

- **A faster PHY rate** shrinks only the data part. Going from 17 µs to 8.5 µs of data per access barely changes a 217 µs access, so efficiency falls further and throughput hardly improves.
- **Sending more data per access** spreads the same overhead across more bytes. With 64 frames in one access, about 1,070 µs of data shares the 200 µs overhead, so roughly 84% of the airtime carries data.

**Frame aggregation** does the second. An **A-MPDU** packs many frames into one transmission, and a **Block Ack** acknowledges them together, so the access cost is paid once. It is one of the most important efficiency mechanisms in Wi-Fi 4 and later, but the gain depends on having enough queued data for the same receiver: sparse, latency-sensitive traffic cannot always be aggregated. No single efficiency percentage holds for every link.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A car ferry with a fixed crossing time
> A ferry spends the same time docking, lowering its ramp and crossing whether it carries one car or forty; only driving the cars on and off grows with the load. Sailing with one car wastes nearly the whole trip. Hiring quicker drivers who board in half the time hardly helps, but filling the deck makes every crossing count.
>
> **How it maps:** Each crossing is one channel access, and the docking and crossing time is the fixed overhead. Driving cars on and off is the data airtime, so quicker drivers are a higher PHY rate, which shrinks only that small part. Filling the deck is frame aggregation.
>
> **Where it stops:** A ferry's crossing time does not change with traffic, but Wi-Fi's backoff and retries grow when the channel is busy. One damaged frame in an aggregate can be retransmitted on its own, whereas a ferry does not send a single car back across.

## Key takeaways
- A fixed channel-access cost overwhelms a short frame but can be shared by an aggregate.
- At high PHY rates, aggregation improves efficiency far more than an even faster rate.
- The 200-microsecond model omits variable per-frame overhead and is not a measured efficiency guarantee.

## Further reading
- [WiFi — High Performance Browser Networking](https://hpbn.co/wifi/)
- [Cisco: Wi-Fi throughput validation and PHY-rate tables](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/wireless-mobility/wireless-lan-wlan/212892-802-11ac-wireless-throughput-testing-and.html)

questions.prompt: A client's link sends 1,500-byte frames, each taking about 17 µs of data airtime, and every channel access costs about 200 µs of fixed overhead (DIFS, backoff, preamble, SIFS, acknowledgment). Throughput is poor. Which change would raise throughput the most?

options.text: Double the PHY rate, so each frame takes about 8.5 µs
options.explanation: Doubling the rate shrinks only the 17 µs data part of a roughly 217 µs access. The 200 µs overhead still dominates, so throughput rises by only a few per cent.

options.text: Aggregate about 32 frames into each channel access with a Block Ack
options.explanation: Correct. The 200 µs overhead is now paid once for about 544 µs of data, so the share of airtime carrying data rises from about 8% to roughly 73%.

options.text: Lengthen DIFS so collisions are less likely
options.explanation: A longer fixed gap adds overhead to every access. It does not address the fact that each access carries very little data.

options.text: Send each frame twice so lost frames need no retransmission
options.explanation: Duplicating frames doubles the airtime used per byte delivered. The fixed overhead is still paid for every access.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare the two parts of one access: about 17 µs of data and about 200 µs of fixed overhead. Overhead is over 90% of the airtime.
2. A faster PHY rate shrinks only the data part. Even halving 17 µs leaves the access at about 208 µs, so the delivered rate barely changes.
3. Aggregation keeps the overhead fixed but fills the access with more data. With 32 frames, about 544 µs of data shares the same 200 µs overhead: roughly 73% efficiency instead of about 8%.
4. So when per-access overhead dominates, sending more per access beats sending each frame faster. Real overhead also includes per-frame delimiters and padding, and aggregation needs enough queued data for the same receiver.

lessons.title: Sharing airtime and diagnosing slow Wi-Fi
lessons.summary: Equal frame opportunities can give a slow active client disproportionate airtime in the simplified DCF model.
lessons.body:
One slow device can make a whole Wi-Fi network feel slow, and a fast download can make every video call stutter. Both come from the same fact: stations share airtime, not bits.

## Half duplex and sharing

An ordinary single radio link cannot simultaneously transmit and receive on that link. Uploads and downloads consume the same radio resources; scheduling, OFDMA/MU-MIMO, spatial reuse and multiple links make modern sharing more complex than a single global turn-taking sequence.

## The performance anomaly

In a simplified saturated, equal-priority DCF model with comparable frame sizes, stations obtain similar *access opportunities*, not similar *airtime*. A slow station's frames take much longer on air, so it uses most of the time, and every faster station is dragged down towards its pace.

> [!example] One slow client
> A fast client at 54 Mbit/s and a slow one at 6 Mbit/s alternate 1,500-byte frames, ignoring overhead. The fast frame takes about 0.22 ms and the slow one 2 ms, so each cycle of 2.22 ms moves one frame for each. **Both** get about 5.4 Mbit/s: the fast client loses 90% of its potential throughput.

The model assumes both clients always have a frame waiting and get equal turns. The result is called the **performance anomaly**. A client at the edge of coverage, using a low MCS, is the usual culprit.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: One till, taking turns
> Two shoppers share a single till and take strict turns, one item each. One scans in a second; the other pays for each item in coins and takes ten seconds. Both leave at the same slow rate, because every turn includes the slow customer's ten seconds.
>
> **How it maps:** The till is the shared channel, each item is a frame, and strict turns are DCF's equal access opportunities. The coin-paying shopper is the low-rate client whose frames occupy far more airtime, and both leaving at the same rate is equal per-station throughput. Giving each shopper equal *time* at the till instead of equal turns is airtime fairness.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real Wi-Fi turns are random rather than strictly alternating, aggregation lets a station move many frames per turn, and the AP controls downlink scheduling far more than uplink.

Some APs implement **airtime fairness** policies to mitigate this; capabilities and effectiveness vary. Moving compatible clients to another band can separate contention, but does not guarantee high rates there.

## Loss, retries and queues

Interference and fading cause corrupted frames. Wi-Fi retries at the link layer, which can hide some radio losses from TCP but adds latency and jitter. Under load, large buffers in the AP add more: an illustrative loaded link might show 5 ms idle RTT and 200 ms during a download; this is not a universal measurement or unique diagnosis. Queueing delay is the time needed to drain what is already waiting: 2 MB queued ahead of a packet on an 80 Mbit/s link adds about 0.2 s, however short the radio path.

## Practical consequences
- Survey placement, interference, client capabilities and backhaul before changing configuration. Wired backhaul avoids consuming wireless backhaul airtime; a dedicated radio still has coexistence and capacity constraints.
- Compare permitted bands for the actual devices and coverage needs. Extra APs need channel and power planning; more is not automatically better.
- Wired connections can remove active traffic from radio contention. An idle device’s removal need not produce a measurable improvement.
- Compare local wired and wireless tests, RSSI/SNR, negotiated rates, retries, airtime use and loaded latency to locate the bottleneck.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Universal handset stream counts, fixed TCP efficiency ratios, driver defaults and guaranteed channel-plan outcomes are omitted because they need device-specific evidence. Regional spectrum rules are time-sensitive; consult the regulator before deployment. No RF, coverage, interference or throughput measurements were performed for this lesson.

## Key takeaways
- Equal frame opportunities can give a slow active client disproportionate airtime in the simplified DCF model.
- Separate airtime, retries, queueing and backhaul with measurements before changing a deployment.

## Further reading
- [WiFi — High Performance Browser Networking](https://hpbn.co/wifi/)
- [Heusse et al.: Performance Anomaly of 802.11b](https://web.cs.wpi.edu/~rek/Nets2/C10/Performance_Anomaly.pdf)

questions.prompt: Two clients share one AP and, in a simplified saturated DCF model, alternate 1,500-byte frames. Client F has a 300 Mbit/s link rate; client S, at the edge of coverage, is at 30 Mbit/s. Ignoring MAC overhead, which prediction about **F's** throughput is right?

options.text: F keeps nearly its full 300 Mbit/s, because S only uses a tenth of the capacity
options.explanation: Each S frame occupies ten times the airtime of an F frame. With equal turns, S uses most of the air, not a tenth.

options.text: F gets about half its link rate, because two clients share the channel
options.explanation: Halving would hold only if both clients had the same link rate. S's slow frames take far more airtime than F's.

options.text: F falls to roughly S's throughput, around a tenth of its own link rate, because every turn includes one of S's long frames
options.explanation: Correct. Each cycle is one short F frame plus one long S frame, so both clients move one frame per cycle and get the same throughput, about 27 Mbit/s here. This is the performance anomaly.

options.text: F is unaffected, since its rate does not depend on S
options.explanation: F and S share one channel and take turns; time S spends on air is time F cannot use.

questions.workedExample:
1. Equal turns, not equal time: in the model each client sends one frame per cycle.
2. Airtime per frame is the frame size divided by the link rate. F's frame takes about 40 µs; S's, at a tenth of the rate, takes about 400 µs.
3. One cycle therefore lasts about 440 µs and moves one frame for each client, about 27 Mbit/s each.
4. F has lost over 90% of its potential 300 Mbit/s and runs at almost the slow client's pace. That is the **performance anomaly**.
5. Airtime fairness, moving S closer or to another AP, or steering capable clients to another band can mitigate it, depending on implementation and traffic direction.

questions.prompt: A busy venue has compatible clients sending small packets plus older 2.4-GHz-only devices. Which measures directly multiplex clients within an access, allocate airtime more fairly, or move clients to separate contention resources, when supported and configured? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enabling OFDMA so the AP serves several clients' small frames in one transmission
options.explanation: Correct. Suitable OFDMA scheduling can multiplex compatible clients into one access; workload and scheduler behaviour determine the benefit.

options.text: Enabling airtime fairness on the APs
options.explanation: Correct as a potential mitigation. Airtime policies and traffic direction determine how much control the AP has; this does not guarantee elimination of every slow-client effect.

options.text: Steering capable clients onto 6 GHz, where legacy devices cannot operate
options.explanation: Correct where permitted and supported. This separates them from older 2.4/5-GHz-only clients, but 6 GHz is not interference-free or guaranteed to use high rates.

options.text: Enabling 1024-QAM
options.explanation: Higher QAM can shorten data airtime when signal quality permits, but does not directly combine clients’ separate channel accesses. Proximity alone is not the criterion.

options.text: Using 40 MHz channels on 2.4 GHz to double capacity
options.explanation: A 40 MHz 2.4 GHz channel consumes more of the available band and leaves fewer separate channels for neighbours. It does not directly provide the per-user scheduling or resource separation requested here; actual interference depends on the deployment.

questions.workedExample: OFDMA can amortise contention, airtime policies can improve scheduling, and another permitted band can separate clients into different contention resources. These are candidates for measurement, not a guaranteed ranking. Higher QAM addresses payload rate, while wider 2.4 GHz channels reduce the separate-channel choices available in a dense deployment.

questions.prompt: With numeric ping output to a home router, measured RTT rises from 4 ms idle to 180–250 ms during a download, without observed loss. Which leading hypothesis should be tested against local queue, retry and CPU measurements?

options.text: The download moves the router's radio to a longer-range channel with more propagation delay
options.explanation: Propagation delay over a few metres is nanoseconds. Channel choice does not add 200 ms.

options.text: The router is rate-limiting ICMP during heavy traffic
options.explanation: A token-bucket drop policy often causes loss, but ICMP scheduling or prioritisation can also affect latency. Do not exclude all router processing effects from the ping trace alone.

options.text: Load-induced queueing, potentially compounded by wireless retries or contention
options.explanation: Correct as a leading hypothesis, not a unique diagnosis. Locate the actual queue before choosing AQM, scheduling or shaping changes.

options.text: DNS lookups during the download slow ping down
options.explanation: With numeric output the measured RTT increase is not explained by reverse-name display lookups. Some ping modes do perform name lookups, so “ping never uses DNS” is too broad.

questions.workedExample:
1. RTT rises only while the download runs, without observed loss. That points to a queue filling somewhere on the path, possibly made worse by wireless retries or contention.
2. Queueing delay is the time needed to drain what is already waiting. As a hypothetical first-in-first-out example, 2 MB queued ahead of a packet on an 80 Mbit/s link adds about 0.2 s, the same order as the observed jump.
3. The ping alone does not measure that backlog or prove all the delay is bufferbloat.
4. Compare a wired test, AP queue and retry counters and how busy the AP's processor is, then choose AQM, scheduling or shaping for the actual bottleneck.

lessons.title: Mobile-core functions and session anchors
lessons.summary: Separate the device, radio access network and core roles.
lessons.body:
Cellular systems centrally schedule much of their radio traffic, unlike basic Wi-Fi contention. This is a distinction in access mechanisms, not a guarantee of collision-free radio or predictable latency: random access, interference, coverage and load still matter. Cellular deployments can use licensed, shared or unlicensed spectrum; Wi-Fi also has scheduled multi-user modes.

For applications, mobile paths introduce changing capacity, radio-state transitions, possible address changes and provider-specific translation or filtering. Design for interruption and measure the devices and networks you support.

## The big picture

Every cellular network has three parts: the phone (the **UE**, user equipment), the **radio access network** (RAN) of base stations, and the **core network** that handles identity, sessions and the packet gateway to the Internet.

```
 UE ~~radio~~ eNodeB/gNodeB
                 |  (backhaul)
     +-----------+----------+
     | Core                 |
     |  control: MME / AMF  |
     |  sessions: SMF       |
     |  user plane:         |
     |  S-GW+P-GW / UPF ----+--> Internet
     +----------------------+
```

| Part | 4G (LTE / EPC) | 5G (NR / 5GC) |
|---|---|---|
| Base station | eNodeB | gNodeB |
| Attach, mobility | MME | AMF |
| Session control | distributed across MME and gateway control functions | 5G SMF (session management function) |
| Packet gateway | S-GW + P-GW | UPF |
| Subscriber data / authentication | HSS with associated authentication functions | UDM/UDR for subscriber data; AUSF for authentication |

The 5G core defines **service-based** control-plane functions with HTTP-based service interfaces. Not every interface is HTTP/2: user-plane tunnels and control interfaces such as N4 use other protocols. Functions can be virtualised; earlier generations also support virtualisation, so “5G software versus 4G fixed boxes” is misleading.

## Tunnels keep your IP address still

For an IP session, session establishment selects/allocates addressing and user-plane resources. LTE uses EPS bearers with a P-GW anchor. In 5G, the session management function manages the PDU session and address allocation, potentially using a UPF or external allocation mechanism; a session-anchor UPF forwards user traffic. Not every PDU session carries IP: Ethernet and unstructured types also exist. Relevant radio-to-core user-plane interfaces use **GTP-U**, whose registered destination UDP port is 2152.

The P-GW or anchor UPF is the **session anchor**: to the Internet, your phone lives there. During a supported handover that preserves the session anchor/address, user-plane paths can be updated while the application retains its IP address. Connections can survive, but radio interruption, loss, session changes or timeout can still break them; no particular vehicle speed guarantees continuity.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A fixed postal address with forwarding
> You keep one published address at a central sorting office while you travel. Letters always go there first, and the office forwards each one to wherever you are staying this week; when you move on, you tell the office and it updates the forwarding instruction. Your correspondents never need to know you moved.
>
> **How it maps:** The published address is the phone's IP address, the sorting office is the session anchor (P-GW or anchor UPF), and the forwarding instruction is the GTP-U tunnel towards the current base station. A handover updates that tunnel, so servers keep sending to the same address.
>
> **Where it stops:** Forwarding happens per packet in milliseconds, not per letter in days, and the network coordinates the update rather than the traveller writing in. Letters in transit during a move can be lost or delayed, just as packets can be during a handover, and a different provider's network (such as home Wi-Fi) has no arrangement with this sorting office.

Moving to an independently addressed Wi-Fi path commonly changes the effective endpoint address. Keeping the old path alive, provider-integrated access, tunnels or mobility-capable transports can change the outcome.

## Key takeaways
- Separate the device, radio access network and core roles.
- Supported anchored handovers can retain an IP address; interruption and session changes can still break a connection.

options.explanation: A handover changes the serving radio resources and can occur between cells of the same base station. Session anchoring and path updates, rather than an assumed base-station address assignment, explain the retained address.

options.text: A preserved session anchor—P-GW in LTE or session-anchor UPF in 5G—with updated user-plane paths
options.explanation: Correct. Retaining the session’s addressing while updating radio-side paths can preserve connectivity; not every handover preserves every session.

options.text: DHCP leases that last longer than the journey
options.explanation: A long lease alone does not redirect the user-plane path during handover. Address-allocation methods can vary, including external mechanisms; anchoring and mobility procedures are the relevant distinction.

Continuity is possible under the stated observation, not guaranteed for all handovers.

lessons.title: Radio scheduling, numerology and 5G options
lessons.summary: Twelve subcarriers set a resource block’s frequency width; spacing and time allocation are separate dimensions.
lessons.body:
Wi-Fi stations mostly decide for themselves when to transmit. A cellular base station instead acts as a central scheduler, telling each phone which slices of frequency and time it may use. That design choice shapes how 4G and 5G handle many users, and why 5G can offer much shorter scheduling intervals.

## Scheduled radio access

LTE and NR divide the channel into a grid of frequency and time. In frequency, a **resource block** spans **12 subcarriers**: with LTE's 15 kHz subcarrier spacing that is 180 kHz. In time, conventional LTE schedules in 1 ms subframes. The base station's scheduler assigns resource blocks in each interval to particular phones, based on their demand, radio conditions and the operator's policy. Later features and specialised modes qualify a universal 1 ms rule, and LTE uplink commonly uses DFT-spread OFDM (SC-FDMA) rather than simply the downlink waveform.

For dynamically scheduled uplink data without an existing grant, a connected UE can request resources and receive an uplink grant. Existing/configured grants and random-access procedures mean a fresh request/grant is not required for every packet. Scheduling coordinates access but does not eliminate random-access collisions or inter-cell interference; fairness is a scheduler policy, not an automatic guarantee.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Air traffic control versus an uncontrolled airfield
> At a small uncontrolled airfield, pilots listen to the radio, announce themselves and slot in when the circuit looks clear. At a busy airport, a controller assigns each aircraft a runway slot, and pilots must request clearance before moving.
>
> **How it maps:** The uncontrolled airfield is Wi-Fi's listen-and-wait contention. The controller is the base station's scheduler, a runway slot is a set of resource blocks in one time interval, and requesting clearance is the scheduling request and uplink grant.
>
> **Where it stops:** Even at a controlled airport the first call to the tower can clash with another aircraft's call, just as cellular random access can collide. Unlike separate airports, neighbouring cells commonly reuse the same frequencies, so one cell's transmissions can interfere with its neighbours'.

## 5G numerology: shorter slots

5G NR adds flexible **numerology**: the subcarrier spacing can be 15, 30, 60 or 120 kHz in common configurations (later releases add more). Each doubling of the spacing halves the OFDM symbol duration, and so halves the slot:

```formula reference
Δf = 15 kHz × 2^μ
T_slot = 1 ms / (2^μ)
where
Δf: delta-f, the subcarrier spacing, in kilohertz (kHz)
μ: mu, the numerology index, a whole number: 0, 1, 2 or 3 in these examples; 2^μ means 2 raised to the power μ, so 1, 2, 4 or 8
T_slot: the duration of one full slot with normal cyclic prefix (14 OFDM symbols), in milliseconds (ms)
kHz: kilohertz, one thousand hertz
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
In words: doubling the subcarrier spacing makes each symbol, and so each slot, half as long.
```

| Spacing | Slot length | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| 15 kHz | 1 ms | low band, wide coverage |
| 30 kHz | 0.5 ms | mid band (e.g. 3.5 GHz) |
| 60 kHz | 0.25 ms | some mid and high bands |
| 120 kHz | 0.125 ms | mmWave |

What changes when the spacing goes up:

- **More frequent scheduling opportunities.** Shorter slots let the scheduler react and grant resources more often. Mini-slot transmission need not occupy a full slot. This helps latency, but does not by itself guarantee lower latency for applications.
- **More tolerance of frequency error.** Wider spacing makes a given frequency offset or phase noise smaller relative to the gap between subcarriers, which matters at high frequencies.
- **Less tolerance of echoes.** The cyclic prefix shrinks with the symbol, so it can absorb less **delay spread** (the time between a signal and its reflections). Wide spacing therefore suits smaller cells, where reflections arrive close together. That is one reason low bands with wide coverage use narrow spacing.

## Spectrum: coverage versus capacity

NR specifications define release-specific frequency ranges, with different supported bandwidths and spacings:

- **FR1** includes low and mid bands. Lower frequencies often aid coverage, while wider available allocations can provide capacity; actual range depends on power, antennas and surroundings. A 3.5 GHz deployment is an illustrative mid-band case, not a universal regional allocation.
- **FR2** covers higher-frequency NR bands, commonly called mmWave in the industry, and has release-specific subdivisions. Wide channels and beamforming can support high capacity, but blockage and link budget matter. A fixed “few hundred metres” coverage rule is not reliable for every deployment.

> [!note] Why "5G" on your phone may be mostly 4G
> A common **NSA option 3** deployment uses LTE/EPC as the master/core with NR as secondary access. **SA option 2** connects NR to the 5G core. “NSA” has broader architectural usage, and a status icon alone does not prove which capabilities are active. Feature availability depends on release, configuration, device and operator support.

ITU IMT-2020 evaluation requirements include a 20 Gbit/s peak downlink data rate and 4 ms eMBB / 1 ms URLLC user-plane latency targets under their defined conditions. The latency measure is one-way radio user-plane latency, not an Internet ping RTT; the peak rate is not a per-user service guarantee. Scheduling, backhaul, core routing, server work and other parts of the path contribute to application latency.

### 5G-Advanced and what comes next

3GPP standards arrive in numbered releases. 5G-Advanced began with Release 18 (functionally frozen in 2024), and 3GPP calls Release 19 (completed in late 2025) the second 5G-Advanced release. In 2026 3GPP was working on Release 20, which carries further 5G-Advanced features alongside the first 6G studies; 3GPP plans normative 6G specifications for Release 21. These schedules change, so check 3GPP's releases page for the current status. Whether a phone or network supports a feature depends on what each operator and vendor actually deploys, not on the release number alone.

## Key takeaways
- A central scheduler allocates resource blocks in frequency and time; twelve subcarriers set a resource block's width.
- NR spacing and normal-prefix slot duration scale together; release and deployment determine supported features.

questions.prompt: An operator configures an NR carrier with 120 kHz subcarrier spacing instead of 30 kHz, keeping the normal cyclic prefix. Which prediction is correct?

options.text: Slots become four times longer, so the scheduler reacts more slowly
options.explanation: The relationship is inverse: each doubling of spacing halves the symbol and slot. Going from 30 to 120 kHz is two doublings, so slots get four times shorter.

options.text: Slots become a quarter as long (0.5 ms to 0.125 ms), giving more frequent scheduling opportunities, while the shorter cyclic prefix tolerates less echo spread
options.explanation: Correct. Wider spacing shortens symbols and slots, which suits high-frequency, smaller cells. It also makes frequency errors relatively smaller, but the shorter cyclic prefix copes with less multipath delay spread. Lower application latency is possible, not guaranteed.

options.text: Coverage improves, because wider spacing carries signals further
options.explanation: Range depends mainly on frequency band, power and antennas. Wide spacing is typically used for high bands with small cells, not to extend coverage.

options.text: Nothing changes, because NR slot length is fixed at 1 ms like LTE
options.explanation: NR deliberately scales the slot with the numerology: 1, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 ms for 15, 30, 60 and 120 kHz.

questions.workedExample:
1. In NR numerology, each doubling of the subcarrier spacing halves the OFDM symbol duration, and so halves the slot.
2. 30 kHz to 120 kHz is two doublings, so the slot shrinks from 0.5 ms to 0.125 ms.
3. Shorter slots mean the scheduler gets more opportunities per second to grant resources, which can reduce radio scheduling delay. Backhaul, core and server delays still add to application latency.
4. Wider spacing makes a given frequency offset or phase noise relatively smaller, useful at mmWave. The cyclic prefix shrinks with the symbol, so it tolerates less echo delay, which suits small cells.
5. Spacing does not by itself extend coverage; wide spacing usually goes with high bands and short range.

options.explanation: Correct. Moving to a suitable 5GC deployment enables the relevant framework, but does not itself guarantee application latency or isolation.

options.text: NSA phones cannot reach the Internet without Wi-Fi
options.explanation: NSA phones have full Internet access; the control plane simply runs over LTE.

options.text: Slicing requires mmWave
options.explanation: Slicing is a core and orchestration feature independent of frequency band.
