questions.prompt: An API gateway fails to allocate resources for new outbound TCP connections while established traffic continues. OS diagnostics point to new-flow resource pressure rather than a path-wide outage. Which are direct resource-exhaustion candidates? Select all that apply.

options.text: The connection-tracking (conntrack) or NAT table on the host or a NAT gateway is full
options.explanation: Correct as a candidate. New tracked flows require capacity. Linux conntrack may emit a rate-limited table-full message; a remote NAT gateway has its own telemetry, and logging is not guaranteed for every failure.

options.text: Ephemeral port exhaustion: many short connections to the same backend address leave sockets in TIME_WAIT, so no source ports are free
options.explanation: Correct as a candidate. Automatic source-port allocation and reusable tuples are finite; TIME_WAIT and active connections can consume them. Pooling or reuse may reduce pressure, while actual remedies depend on the measured allocation policy and limit.

options.text: An MTU black hole on the path to the backends
options.explanation: A PMTU problem is a path/packet-size issue, not direct exhaustion of the new-flow allocation resources specified here. It can affect setup or later protocol data in other circumstances.

options.text: Long RTT to the backends
options.explanation: RTT alone is not an exhausted allocation resource, though long connection lifetimes and short application deadlines can contribute to pressure or failures.

questions.workedExample:
1. The symptom is new connections failing while established ones continue, so look for a resource consumed per new flow.
2. **Conntrack/NAT tables**: every new tracked flow needs an entry; when the table is full, new flows fail. Linux may log a rate-limited 'table full' message, and a NAT gateway has its own metrics.
3. **Ephemeral ports**: each connection to the same destination address and port needs a distinct local port, and a closed connection keeps its port in TIME_WAIT for a while (60 s by default on Linux). As a rough single-destination illustration, Linux's default range of 28,232 ports held for 60 s each supports only about 470 new connections per second. Configuration, extra source addresses and tuple reuse change this, so use errors and counters to find the real limit.
4. Connection pooling or reuse reduces pressure on both.
5. An MTU black hole and long RTT are real problems, but neither is a per-flow allocation resource running out.

lessons.title: Loss-limited and window-limited TCP models
lessons.summary: The periodic-loss Reno model has explicit assumptions and does not describe every congestion control.
lessons.body:
A single TCP connection can be far slower than the link it runs over. Two simple models predict why: one says loss and distance limit throughput, the other says the window of data in flight does. Knowing which applies tells you what to fix.

## Loss-limited throughput

Loss-based TCP grows its congestion window by about one segment per round trip and roughly halves it at each loss. Two things follow. A longer round trip means slower growth, and more frequent loss means the window is cut before it gets large. The simplified **Mathis model** for Reno congestion avoidance captures both:

```formula essential
X ≈ (MSS / RTT)(1.22 / √(p))
where
X: the model's long-run throughput for one TCP flow, in bits per second (bit/s)
MSS: maximum segment size: the most payload in one TCP segment, in bits for this formula (1,460 bytes is 11,680 bits)
RTT: the round-trip time, in seconds (s)
p: the packet loss probability as a fraction, e.g. 0.0001 for one packet in 10,000
√: square root
1.22: approximately the square root of 3/2, which comes from the saw-tooth shape of Reno's window
≈: approximately equal to
In words: throughput is one segment per round trip, multiplied by a factor that grows as loss gets rarer; doubling the RTT halves throughput, while cutting loss by 100 times only raises it 10 times.
```

What it predicts:

- **Distance hurts directly.** The same 0.01% loss gives about 14 Mbit/s at 100 ms RTT but about 140 Mbit/s at 10 ms. A transfer that is fine within a city can crawl across an ocean with exactly the same loss rate.
- **Loss hurts by its square root.** Halving the loss rate raises throughput by only about 40%. Tiny loss rates, invisible to a short ping test, can still cap a long-distance flow.
- **A single flow can be far below link capacity** even when nothing is "wrong" with the link.

The model assumes periodic loss, one ACK per segment, enough data and window, light-to-moderate loss and no timeout-dominated behaviour. It describes classic Reno; CUBIC and especially BBR respond to loss differently, so treat it as an explanation of the trend, not a prediction for every stack. Parallel streams can hide per-flow limits, so compare single- and multi-stream tests with endpoint measurements.

## Window-limited throughput

Without loss, a single flow is capped at **one window per round trip**: the sender can have at most one window of unacknowledged data in flight, and must wait about a round trip for acknowledgments before sending more. To fill a link, the window must be at least the link rate times the RTT, the **bandwidth-delay product** (BDP).

```formula reference
X_max = (8W) / RTT
where
X_max: the window-limited throughput, in bits per second (bit/s)
W: the effective window: the unacknowledged data allowed in flight, in bytes (B)
RTT: the round-trip time, in seconds (s)
B: byte, 8 bits; multiplying by 8 converts bytes to bits
In words: a flow can send at most one window per round trip, so its throughput limit is the window divided by the round-trip time, whatever the link speed.
```

For example, filling 1 Gbit/s at 100 ms RTT needs 12.5 MB in flight, while a flow limited to a 4 MB window at that RTT tops out around 320 Mbit/s even on a 10 Gbit/s link. The effective window is the smaller of the congestion window and the receiver's advertised window; socket-memory limits influence both but are not identical to either. If a long-distance flow is window-limited, upgrading the link does nothing, while raising the window limits (for example receive-buffer autotuning limits) does.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Fixed SYN retry schedules, universal timeout advice and diagnoses inferred from one counter or trace are intentionally omitted. Sample outputs are illustrative. Real-device captures, WAN impairments and production incident causes were not measured in this review.

## Key takeaways
- The periodic-loss Reno model has explicit assumptions and does not describe every congestion control.
- An effective flight window divided by RTT is a per-flow limit, so long paths need large windows to fill fast links.

## Further reading
- [Mathis et al.: The Macroscopic Behavior of the TCP Congestion Avoidance Algorithm](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~lam/395t/papers/Mathis1998.pdf)
- [Linux TCP configuration: windows, timeouts and recovery](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/ip-sysctl.html)

questions.prompt:
In the ideal Reno Mathis model, a TCP flow's throughput is:

```formula
X ≈ (MSS / RTT)(1.22 / √(p))
where
X: the flow's long-run throughput, in bits per second (bit/s)
MSS: maximum segment size, in bits
RTT: round-trip time, in seconds (s)
p: the loss probability as a fraction
√: square root
≈: approximately equal to
In words: one segment per round trip, multiplied by a factor that grows as loss becomes rarer.
```

A long-distance backup flow is loss-limited. You can afford one change: halve the RTT (by moving the backup target closer) or halve the loss rate (by fixing a noisy link). Which raises this model's throughput more?

options.text: Halving the loss rate, because throughput is proportional to the loss rate
options.explanation: Throughput depends on the square root of the loss rate, not the loss rate itself. Halving loss raises it by only about 1.41 times.

options.text: Halving the RTT: throughput doubles, while halving loss raises it only about 1.41 times
options.explanation: Correct. RTT appears directly in the denominator, so halving it doubles the model's throughput. Loss enters through its square root, and the square root of 2 is about 1.41.

options.text: Both give exactly the same improvement
options.explanation: RTT and loss enter the model differently: one directly, one through a square root.

options.text: Neither helps, because TCP throughput depends only on link capacity
options.explanation: A single loss-limited flow can run far below link capacity; this model describes exactly that case.

questions.workedExample:
1. Read the shape of the model rather than plugging in numbers: RTT divides the whole expression, and the loss rate appears under a square root.
2. Halving RTT therefore doubles throughput: the average window, which the loss rate sets, stays the same size, but each window is delivered twice as often.
3. Halving the loss rate multiplies the loss factor by the square root of 2, about 1.41: the window gets somewhat larger before each cut.
4. So in this model, distance matters more than modest loss improvements; moving data closer, or using more parallel flows, often beats chasing small loss reductions.
5. This is a Reno model result. CUBIC and BBR respond differently, and real paths have other limits.

questions.prompt: A single backlogged TCP flow over a 10 Gbit/s path with a fixed 80 ms RTT reaches only about 400 Mbit/s. There is no loss, the link is otherwise idle, and `ss` shows the flight window pinned at about 4 MB, set by the receiver's maximum receive buffer. Which change would raise this flow's throughput?

options.text: Upgrade the path to 100 Gbit/s
options.explanation: The flow is not using the existing capacity. It is limited to one 4 MB window per 80 ms round trip, whatever the link speed.

options.text: Raise the receiver's maximum receive buffer (and so its window) towards the bandwidth-delay product
options.explanation: Correct. With no loss, throughput is about one window per round trip: 4 MB per 80 ms is about 400 Mbit/s. Filling 10 Gbit/s at 80 ms needs about 100 MB in flight.

options.text: Switch congestion control to a loss-based algorithm
options.explanation: There is no loss and the limit is the receiver's window, not congestion control's response to loss.

options.text: Reduce packet loss on the path
options.explanation: There is no loss to reduce; the window, not loss, is the binding limit.

questions.workedExample:
1. With no loss, a sender can have at most one window of unacknowledged data in flight and must wait about a round trip for acknowledgments. So the limit is roughly one window per round trip.
2. 4 MB per 80 ms round trip is about 400 Mbit/s, matching the measurement, so the window is the bottleneck.
3. Keeping a 10 Gbit/s, 80 ms path full would need about 100 MB in flight (the bandwidth-delay product), 25 times this window.
4. Since `ss` shows the receiver's buffer limit setting the window, raising that limit (for example receive-buffer autotuning maxima) is the change that helps. A faster link or loss fixes change nothing while the window is the binding limit.
5. Socket-memory limits, advertised receive window and cwnd are distinct, so confirm which one is binding before changing configuration.

questions.prompt: A capture of a slow file upload shows the **server** repeatedly advertising a TCP window of 0, the client sending window probes, then a burst of data each time the window opens. RTT is low and there are no retransmissions. Which constraint is directly evidenced, and where should investigation start?

options.text: Packet loss on the network
options.explanation: The supplied trace directly establishes the advertised receive window closing to zero. It does not establish packet loss as its cause; lack of observed retransmissions alone cannot exclude every loss elsewhere.

options.text: The client's congestion window is too small
options.explanation: The congestion window limits the sender, but here the *receiver* is explicitly saying it has no room.

options.text: Receiver flow control is stopping new data; investigate application consumption and receive-side resource/window policy
options.explanation: Correct. A zero advertised window is not a raw free-memory reading and does not prove slow disk or a blocked application is the only cause.

options.text: An MTU black hole
options.explanation: The advertised zero window directly constrains new data. A separate PMTU issue may coexist, but it is not what the specified window advertisements establish.

questions.workedExample: A zero advertised receive window permits no further ordinary new data in that window. The sender’s probes and later bursts are consistent with flow-control stalls. Inspect receive queues, memory limits, window behaviour and application consumption. The trace does not uniquely identify the server’s disk, nor prove there are no other network problems.

lessons.title: Autonomous systems and commercial routing policy
lessons.summary: BGP carries policy-controlled reachability; AS-path length is not latency.
lessons.body:
"The Internet" is not one network. It comprises independently administered networks exchanging traffic under their routing policies, connected by physical cables under streets and oceans, by switches in shared buildings, and increasingly by satellites.

To reason about latency, outages, costs and why your packets take the route they do, you need the physical and the commercial picture together: who connects to whom, why, over what, and how fast light can get there.

## Autonomous systems and BGP

The unit of the Internet is the **autonomous system** (AS): a network under one administration with its own routing policy, identified by an AS number. An organisation may operate one AS, several ASes, or use another organisation’s routing. Observed AS/prefix counts depend on date, collector and filtering; no undated count is used here.

ASes exchange reachability with **BGP** (Border Gateway Protocol). BGP announcements carry reachability attributes, including **AS_PATH** information. They can be incorrect or manipulated, and AS-path prepending means the attribute is not a simple record of physical routers. BGP chooses routes by **policy** first (business relationships, configured preferences) and only then by things like AS path length. It does not measure latency or bandwidth.

## Transit, peering and the tiers

Two kinds of business relationship connect ASes:

- **Transit**: a customer pays a provider to provide broad Internet reachability according to the service agreement. A full table or default route may be supplied; policy, filtering, partial-transit products and outages qualify “every destination”.
- **Peering**: two networks exchange traffic *between their own networks and customers only*, under agreed policy. **Settlement-free** peering has no traffic-exchange payment between the peers, while ports, circuits and colocation still cost money. Paid peering also exists; equal benefit is not guaranteed.

This creates a loose hierarchy:

```
   [Tier 1] ==peer== [Tier 1]
      |                  |
   transit            transit
      |                  |
   [Tier 2] ==peer== [Tier 2]
      |                  |
   [access ISP]     [content]
```

- **Tier 1** networks can reach every destination without paying anyone for transit: they peer with all other Tier 1s and have their own customers. This is a commercial/topological classification, not an IETF-certified membership list or proof of uninterrupted reachability.
- **Tier 2** networks peer widely but still buy some transit.
- **Tier 3** or stub networks buy transit and do little peering.

## Routing follows the money

A common economic routing model prefers customer routes over peer/provider routes and restricts export. Some operators further prefer peers over providers, but this is policy rather than a BGP requirement. In the simplified export model:

| Learned from | Exported to |
|---|---|
| Customer | everyone |
| Peer | customers only |
| Provider | customers only |

Under these model assumptions, networks do not offer transit between peers/providers. This produces **valley-free** paths: up through providers, at most one peering link across, then down through customers. Real agreements and traffic engineering can deviate from the model. Policy-selected paths need not minimise distance or latency.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A national courier and a neighbourly swap
> A small shop pays a national courier to deliver its parcels anywhere in the country. It also agrees with the shop next door to hand over parcels for each other's own local customers for free. It would never agree to carry the neighbour's parcels to a third town for free: that is exactly the service the courier charges for.
>
> **How it maps:** The paid courier is a transit provider, and the free swap is settlement-free peering, limited to each other's own customers. Refusing to carry the neighbour's parcels onward unpaid is the export rule that peer routes go only to paying customers, which produces valley-free paths.
>
> **Where it stops:** Networks swap reachability announcements, not physical parcels, and real contracts include paid peering, partial transit and selective exports. Peering is free of traffic charges but not of costs: ports, circuits and colocation still cost money.

> [!warning] Route leaks and hijacks
> BGP trusts announcements by default. In 2008 Pakistan Telecom announced a more specific prefix for YouTube, intended for local blocking; it leaked to its upstream and took YouTube offline for much of the world for hours. In 2019 a small network leaked routes it had learned from one provider to its other provider, Verizon, which accepted them, and significant traffic for Cloudflare and others was drawn through a tiny network. **RPKI route origin validation** checks prefix/origin authorisation against validated ROA information; it does not authenticate the whole AS path or detect every route leak. Local rejection policy, customer prefix filters, relationship-aware controls and monitoring provide complementary defences.

## Forwarding chooses the longest installed prefix

Choosing among BGP routes and looking up a destination are separate steps. After routes have been accepted and installed, ordinary IP forwarding chooses the most specific matching destination prefix. For example, an installed route for `192.0.2.0/24` is preferred for a destination in that range over a covering `192.0.0.0/22`, even if the larger block has a shorter AS-path attribute. Prefix and origin filtering determine whether the advertisement is accepted in the first place.

The addresses here are a hypothetical routing example, not an instruction to announce address space.

## Key takeaways
- BGP carries policy-controlled reachability; AS-path length is not latency.
- Commercial export models produce valley-free paths under their assumptions.
- Origin validation checks authorised origins, not the whole AS path.

## Further reading
- [Autonomous system (Internet) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_system_(Internet))
- [Tier 1 network — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tier_1_network)
- [Peering — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peering)
- [Gao and Rexford: Stable Internet Routing Without Global Coordination](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall14/cos561/papers/StableBGP01.pdf)
- [RFC 4271: BGP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4271)

questions.prompt: A small regional ISP pays a large carrier every month so that its customers can reach any address on the Internet. It also swaps traffic for free with a neighbouring ISP, but only for each other's own customers. What are these two relationships?

options.text: Both are peering: one paid, one settlement-free
options.explanation: Peering is defined by *scope* (each other's customers only), not just by price. Paying for reach to the whole Internet is transit, even though paid peering also exists.

options.text: The first is peering, the second is transit
options.explanation: In this scenario the broad onward-reachability service is transit; the limited neighbour exchange is peering. Actual reachability remains subject to policy and failures.

options.text: The first is transit, the second is settlement-free peering
options.explanation: Correct. The paid broad-reachability service is transit. The agreed exchange of the neighbours’ own/customer traffic has no traffic settlement payment, so it is settlement-free peering.

options.text: Both are transit, because traffic crosses another network in each case
options.explanation: Crossing another network does not make it transit. What matters is whether the other network will carry your traffic onward to the rest of the Internet.

questions.workedExample: The paid service provides broad onward Internet reachability: full transit in this scenario. The neighbour exchange is limited to agreed customer-network reachability and has no settlement payment: settlement-free peering. Transit can supply a default route rather than a full table, peering need not give equal benefits, and both arrangements still have infrastructure costs.

questions.prompt: You run ISP X. You learn a route to 203.0.113.0/24 from a **peer**, Y. Following the usual commercial export rules, which neighbours do you announce it to?

options.text: Everyone: customers, peers and providers
options.explanation: Only routes learned from *customers* go to everyone. Announcing a peer's route to your other peers or providers would invite them to send traffic through you for free.

options.text: Your peers and providers, but not your customers
options.explanation: This is backwards. Your customers pay you for reach, so they get the peer's routes; your peers and providers do not.

options.text: Nobody: peer routes are for your own use only
options.explanation: Under the stated model, eligible peer routes are made available to customers. A customer using a default route need not receive each specific prefix individually.

options.text: Your customers only
options.explanation: Correct. Peer routes are exported only to customers. You carry that traffic because a paying customer is at one end.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask: if I announce this route to a neighbour, who would end up carrying traffic, and who pays?
2. **To a customer**: the customer sends traffic to you, you deliver it to Y over the free peering link. The customer pays you. Good.
3. **To another peer Z**: Z sends traffic to you, you hand it to Y. Nobody pays you, and you spend capacity on traffic between two other networks. Bad.
4. **To a provider**: worse still. You would pay your provider for traffic it sends you, only to deliver it free to Y.

| Learned from | Exported to |
|---|---|
| Customer | everyone |
| Peer | customers only |
| Provider | customers only |

These are the question’s commercial export assumptions. Actual contracts, selective exports, paid peering and other policies can differ.

questions.prompt: Verified path information shows London-to-London traffic taking a detour via Amsterdam. Which mechanisms could explain that route? Select all that apply.

options.text: The user's ISP prefers a route learned from a customer or peer over one learned from a provider, even when the provider route is geographically shorter
options.explanation: Correct. Configured policy can prefer a physically longer route. Customer/peer/provider ordering is an operator choice, not a universal BGP requirement.

options.text: BGP measures latency on each path and has picked the fastest one
options.explanation: BGP has no latency or bandwidth metric. It picks by policy and then attributes such as AS path length, so it can easily pick a slower path.

options.text: The selected interconnection between those networks is in Amsterdam
options.explanation: Correct. The chosen path can detour to that interconnection; other transit routes may also exist.

options.text: With higher-priority attributes equal, a shorter AS_PATH can be preferred even if its physical route is longer
options.explanation: Correct. AS-path length does not measure kilometres; one AS can span a large area.

options.text: All Internet traffic has to pass through a Tier 1 network, and the nearest one is in Amsterdam
options.explanation: There is no requirement for every Internet path to cross a Tier 1. Direct peering and local caches provide counterexamples without needing a global traffic-share claim.

questions.workedExample: Policy preference, selected interconnection location and AS_PATH comparison can each produce geographic detours. BGP does not inherently measure RTT, though external controllers can feed measured information into policy. Reverse paths may differ. Hostnames in traceroute alone would not have established the geography; this question supplies verified path information.

questions.prompt: Network A is a customer of providers P1 and P2. P1 and P2 are both Tier 1s and peer with each other. P1 also peers with P3. Which AS path is consistent with the valley-free rule?

options.text: A → P1 → P2 → a provider of P2
options.explanation: An up step after a peering link violates the stated valley-free model. A route learned by P2 from a provider would not be exported to peer P1; moreover the assumed Tier 1 P2 has no transit provider.

options.text: A → P1 → P2 → a customer of P2
options.explanation: Correct. Up (customer to provider), one peering link across, then down (provider to customer).

options.text: Customer of P1 → P1 → P2 → P3, where P3 peers with P2
options.explanation: This crosses two peering links (P1–P2, then P2–P3). P2 learned the route from a peer, so it would export it only to its customers, not to another peer.

options.text: P1 → A → P2, carrying traffic between A's two providers
options.explanation: This is a valley: down to a customer, then back up. A would be giving free transit between its two providers, and export rules stop it announcing provider routes to another provider.

questions.workedExample:
1. Valley-free means: zero or more steps **up** (customer → provider), at most **one** step **across** a peering link, then zero or more steps **down** (provider → customer).
2. `A → P1 → P2 → cust`: up, across, down. Valid.
3. `cust → P1 → P2 → P3`: up, across, across. For traffic toward P3, P2 learns P3’s route from a peer and would not export it to peer P1 under the model. The forward path therefore cannot be built by those exports. Invalid.
4. `P1 → A → P2`: down then up. A learned P2's routes from a provider, which go only to customers, so P1 never hears them. Invalid.
5. `A → P1 → P2 → provider`: up, across, up. Going up after a peering link breaks the rule, and Tier 1s have no providers to go up to. Invalid.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical network advertises 192.0.0.0/22. A different origin advertises its contained 192.0.2.0/24. A router accepts and installs both routes, with a shorter AS path for the /22. Why does an ordinary destination lookup for 192.0.2.10 use the /24?

options.text: BGP always prefers the most recently received announcement
options.explanation: Age is at most a late tie-breaker between routes for the *same* prefix. It does not explain this.

options.text: The hijacker's AS path was shorter everywhere
options.explanation: The prompt gives the /22 a shorter AS path at this router. AS-path comparison between these distinct prefixes does not override longest-prefix forwarding once both are installed.

options.text: The /22 and /24 are different prefixes, so both are installed, and forwarding uses longest prefix match: the /24 is more specific and wins for every address inside it
options.explanation: Correct under the explicit installation assumptions. Best-route selection is performed per prefix, while the forwarding lookup uses the longest matching installed prefix.

options.text: RPKI marked the real /22 announcement as invalid
options.explanation: RPKI validation is not the longest-prefix mechanism. If covering validated records authorise no matching origin/length, an announcement is Invalid; local policy determines rejection. Another applicable valid record can authorise it.

questions.workedExample: The installed /22 and /24 are different destinations in the routing table. Address 192.0.2.10 matches both, and /24 is the more specific forwarding match. AS-path lengths for these two distinct prefixes are not compared to override that lookup. This is a hypothetical example, not the exact 2008 YouTube timeline. Origin validation and prefix filters can prevent installation of some unauthorised routes, but origin validation does not authenticate an entire path or automatically impose a drop policy.

lessons.title: IXPs, private interconnects and embedded caches
lessons.summary: An IXP fabric can connect many agreed peers through a shared attachment.
lessons.body:
Networks need physical places to meet. Exchange points, private interconnects and caches placed inside ISPs have flattened the old hierarchy, so much of today's traffic never touches a Tier 1 network.

## The flattening of the Internet

Direct interconnection and distributed content delivery add paths outside the simple hierarchy. Content providers can peer with access networks and operate their own transport infrastructure; their footprints and arrangements vary. Netflix's Open Connect and Google Global Cache go further, placing caching servers **inside** ISPs' networks.

Content served inside an ISP or across direct peering need not cross a Tier 1. The fraction of any user’s traffic taking such paths requires measurement.

## Internet exchange points

Peering needs a physical meeting place. An **Internet exchange point** (IXP) is a shared layer 2 switching fabric, often spread across several colocation buildings in a city, where participating networks connect and establish agreed peerings. Sizes, port counts, physical sites and remote-access arrangements differ.

- A shared-fabric port can reach many willing peers, subject to membership and policy, instead of needing a separate physical link for each.
- **Route servers** distribute eligible participant routes according to policy; they normally do not forward the participants’ data traffic. Not every member joins the route server, and joining does not automatically peer with everyone. Redundant sessions are common.
- Large IXPs include DE-CIX Frankfurt, AMS-IX in Amsterdam and LINX in London; traffic peaks are time-sensitive operational measurements, not fixed properties of an IXP.

Networks may use a **private network interconnect** (PNI), such as a dedicated cross-connect or circuit, for capacity or policy reasons. It need not be one fibre in the same building, and there is no universal traffic threshold or majority-share claim here.

## Key takeaways
- An IXP fabric can connect many agreed peers through a shared attachment.
- Route servers exchange routes rather than forwarding participant data.
- Embedded caches and direct peering can keep traffic away from transit paths.

## Further reading
- [Internet exchange point — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_exchange_point)
- [Netflix Open Connect](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)
- [DE-CIX: Peering and route-server participation](https://docs.de-cix.net/article/n3i1zu0abx-how-to-implement-peering-services)

questions.prompt: A regional ISP wants to peer with around 150 networks present in Frankfurt. Why would it connect to an IXP such as DE-CIX rather than running a separate link to each network?

options.text: One port on the shared switching fabric reaches hundreds of peers, and route servers let it peer with many of them over a single BGP session
options.explanation: Correct as the shared-fabric model. Routes depend on participants’ peering policies and route-server filters; connecting does not automatically give every peer’s routes.

options.text: The IXP pays for the ISP's transit
options.explanation: IXP peering itself is not full Internet transit. An exchange operator may sell additional services, but a peering port does not imply free transit.

options.text: Traffic through an IXP is encrypted, unlike a direct link
options.explanation: An IXP is a layer 2 switching fabric. It adds no encryption; that is the job of TLS and similar protocols end to end.

options.text: BGP only works across an IXP
options.explanation: BGP runs over any IP link, including private network interconnects. Large networks often move busy peerings off the IXP onto a PNI.

questions.workedExample: A shared fabric can reach many willing peers without a separate physical link for each. Route servers exchange eligible routes and normally stay out of the data forwarding path; membership and policies limit what is received. Redundant ports/sessions may be needed, and private interconnects remain an option where capacity or policy justifies them.

lessons.title: Submarine resilience and shared access networks
lessons.summary: Independent physical routes and surviving capacity matter more than merely counting logical links.
lessons.body:
Intercontinental Internet traffic depends heavily on fibre-optic cables on the seabed, and most homes reach their ISP over an access network shared with neighbours. Both are physical, finite and sometimes fragile, which shapes outages and evening slow-downs.

## Submarine cables

**Submarine fibre-optic cables** are central to intercontinental connectivity. Traffic shares and cable inventories depend on definitions and date; avoid treating a single unsourced percentage as a universal constant.

How they work:

- Cable systems use **fibre pairs** carrying multiple wavelengths (DWDM). Fibre count and capacity vary by design.
- Long-haul repeatered systems use optical amplifiers at design-specific intervals and shore-fed high-voltage DC power. Shorter unrepeatered systems also exist; spacing and voltage are not universal.
- Modern cables have design capacities in the hundreds of Tbit/s. Google's Dunant cable (US–France, 2021) was announced at 250 Tbit/s.
- Increasingly, cloud and content companies own or co-own cables rather than leasing capacity from telecoms consortia.

ICPC’s June 2025 guidance describes approximately **150–200 faults annually**, with 70–80% attributed to accidental damage, primarily fishing and vessel anchoring. This is a dated industry summary, not a prediction or an exhaustive cause breakdown; other natural and technical causes exist. A marine repair may require a ship to recover the cable and splice it, with timing dependent on fault location, ship availability, weather, permits and the repair method. Networks may reroute over surviving capacity, but regions served by only one or two cables (some island nations, parts of West and East Africa) can lose most connectivity when they are cut.

## The last mile

The **last mile** (or access network) connects homes and businesses to their ISP. It is one possible bottleneck; aggregation networks, interconnection, servers and local Wi-Fi can also limit service.

| Technology | Medium | Rate interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| ADSL / VDSL2 | copper pair | Profile, line quality, length and deployment determine rate |
| DOCSIS cable | shared coaxial cable | Version, spectrum allocation and service plan determine rate |
| GPON fibre | shared optical distribution | Common nominal line rates: 2.48832 Gbit/s down / 1.24416 up; not per-home goodput |
| XGS-PON fibre | shared optical distribution | 10 Gbit/s class (9.95328 Gbit/s nominal each way); shared and before protocol overhead |
| Fixed wireless, 4G/5G | radio | widely variable |

- **DSL** runs over the telephone pair. VDSL2 rates depend on copper length, line quality, profile and interference; shorter runs can support higher rates.
- **Cable** (DOCSIS) shares one coaxial cable network among a neighbourhood, so evening peaks can slow everyone; upload is traditionally much lower than download.
- **PON fibre** (FTTP) shares one fibre from the exchange among optical network terminals via passive splitters. Split ratios and scheduling vary; a marketed access rate is not necessarily a permanently reserved equal fraction.

> [!note] Contention
> Several layers can be oversubscribed: the PON split, the ISP's aggregation network, its transit and peering capacity. Capacity planning often uses busy-hour demand and service commitments rather than assuming every user saturates at once. This is a design choice, not a requirement that every link be oversubscribed. The same principle as data-centre oversubscription, applied to a country.

## Key takeaways
- Independent physical routes and surviving capacity matter more than merely counting logical links.
- PON line capacity is shared and precedes overhead; a service plan is not a permanently reserved share.

## Further reading
- [Submarine communications cable — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_communications_cable)
- [Submarine Cable Map — TeleGeography](https://www.submarinecablemap.com/)
- [Passive optical network — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_optical_network)
- [ICPC: Cable protection and fault summary, June 2025](https://www.iscpc.org/publications/icpc-viewpoints/charting-submarine-cables-is-critical-for-maritime-safety-and-infrastructure-protection/)
- [Google: Dunant ready for service, February 2021](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/infrastructure/googles-dunant-subsea-cable-is-now-ready-for-service)
- [ITU-T G.9807.1: XGS-PON](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-G.9807.1)
- [ITU-T G.984.2: GPON physical layer](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-G.984.2)

questions.prompt: An ISP sells 900 Mbit/s plans to 32 homes sharing one XGS-PON with about 10 Gbit/s downstream. Customers usually get close to 900 Mbit/s in speed tests. What explains this, and when would they notice the sharing?

options.text: Fibre is not shared, so each home always has its own 10 Gbit/s
options.explanation: A PON's downstream is a shared stream split passively among homes. The 10 Gbit/s is the total for the whole split.

options.text: Homes rarely all download at full speed at once, so one busy home can get near its plan rate; if all 32 demanded it simultaneously, they would share about 10 Gbit/s, roughly 300 Mbit/s each with equal sharing
options.explanation: Correct. Together the plans add up to nearly three times the PON's capacity, which works because demand peaks rarely coincide. Real scheduling, overhead and other bottlenecks change the exact share.

options.text: The ISP must be selling only 900 Mbit/s in total across all 32 homes
options.explanation: Plans are sold per home. The point is that their total exceeds the shared capacity, relying on statistical multiplexing.

options.text: Each home gets a fixed 1/32 of the capacity, about 300 Mbit/s, all the time
options.explanation: Shares are not permanently reserved: an idle neighbour's capacity is available to others, which is why speed tests usually reach the plan rate.

questions.workedExample:
1. A PON shares one downstream optical channel among all homes on the split, about 10 Gbit/s for XGS-PON before overhead.
2. 32 plans of 900 Mbit/s add up to 28.8 Gbit/s, nearly three times that capacity: the access network is oversubscribed by design.
3. This works because homes rarely all download flat out at once. A single busy home can get close to its plan rate while others are quiet.
4. In the rare moment when everyone demands their full rate, they share the PON: with equal sharing and no other bottleneck, about 300 Mbit/s each.
5. Real line rates, protocol overhead, scheduler policy and the ISP's aggregation and transit capacity all affect what customers actually see.

questions.prompt: You are planning connectivity for an island nation served by two submarine cables that land on the same stretch of coast. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fishing and anchoring are major documented causes of cable faults, especially where human activity overlaps cable routes
options.explanation: Correct. ICPC’s June 2025 summary attributes 70–80% of recorded faults to accidental damage, primarily fishing and vessel anchoring; other causes also exist.

options.text: Marine repair can be prolonged by ship availability, weather, permits and the work of recovering and splicing cable
options.explanation: Correct. Exact duration and method depend on the fault and system; there is no universal repair deadline.

options.text: Satellites carry most intercontinental traffic, so a cable cut barely matters
options.explanation: Submarine cables are central to intercontinental connectivity. Satellite backup may help, but its available capacity and terminals must be planned rather than assumed sufficient.

options.text: In long-haul repeatered systems, optical amplifiers can receive power from shore-fed high-voltage DC
options.explanation: Correct. Repeater spacing, voltage and design vary, and unrepeatered cable systems also exist.

options.text: With two cables, any single event leaves the country fully connected
options.explanation: Two cables landing in the same place can be cut by one earthquake, landslide or dragged anchor. And even if one survives, it may lack the capacity for all the rerouted traffic.

questions.workedExample: The supported claims concern documented damage mechanisms, repair logistics and shore-fed power in repeatered systems. Two cables sharing a landing area can share physical hazards or terrestrial backhaul. Resilience improves through route/landing diversity and adequate surviving capacity; backup satellites are not an automatic full-capacity substitute.

lessons.title: Fibre propagation and the distance budget
lessons.summary: Propagation follows actual distance and signal speed, separately from queues and processing.
lessons.body:
Bandwidth can be bought; the speed of light cannot. Over long distances, propagation time through fibre sets a floor on round-trip time that no upgrade removes, so distance is often the biggest single factor in latency.

## The physics of latency

Light in glass travels about a third slower than in a vacuum. For signal delay, what counts is the fibre's effective **group index** at the operating wavelength; this lesson assumes 1.47, close to Corning's characterised 1.4682 for SMF-28 Ultra at 1550 nanometres. That gives a speed of roughly 204,000 km/s, about **5 µs per km**.

```formula reference
RTT = (2d) / v
v = c / n
where
RTT: the propagation round-trip time: there and back, ignoring every other delay, in seconds (s)
d: the one-way fibre route length, in kilometres (km)
v: the speed of the signal in the fibre, about 204,000 kilometres per second (km/s)
c: the speed of light in a vacuum, about 299,792 km/s
n: the dimensionless effective group index used for signal delay, assumed to be 1.47 here; the actual value depends on fibre and wavelength
In words: light in fibre covers about 204 km every millisecond, so each 100 km of fibre route adds about 1 ms of round-trip time.
```

A useful rule: **about 1 ms of round-trip time per 100 km of fibre route**. The great-circle distance from London to New York is about 5,570 km, so even an ideal fibre laid along that line would give a propagation RTT of about 55 ms before any router or server adds anything; real cable routes are longer.

What this means in practice:

- **Bandwidth does not fix distance.** A faster link shortens the time to push the bits out, but not the time for them to travel. A ping across an ocean stays near its propagation floor after a 10× bandwidth upgrade.
- **Every round trip pays it again.** Protocols that need several exchanges before any useful data is sent (TCP and TLS handshakes, chains of dependent requests) multiply the distance penalty.
- **Real routes are longer than maps.** Cables follow coastlines and terrain, and return paths can differ, so measured RTTs exceed the map-distance estimate. Transmission, processing and queueing add more.

Shorter routes or nearer servers reduce propagation; reducing queueing can also reduce RTT without changing geography.

## Key takeaways
- Propagation follows actual distance and signal speed, separately from queues and processing.
- Hypothetical route calculations establish conditional bounds, not a measured city-pair RTT.

## Further reading
- [Corning: SMF-28 Ultra optical fibre, including effective group index](https://www.corning.com/content/dam/corning/media/worldwide/coc/documents/Fiber/product-information-sheets/PI-1424-AEN.pdf)
- [BIPM: SI Brochure, including the defined vacuum speed of light](https://www.bipm.org/documents/20126/41483022/SI-Brochure-9.pdf)

questions.prompt: An office measures about 75 ms RTT to a server roughly 5,000 km of fibre route away, with no congestion or loss. Management proposes upgrading the office link from 1 Gbit/s to 10 Gbit/s to "cut the latency". What should you predict?

options.text: RTT drops to about 7.5 ms, because the link is ten times faster
options.explanation: Link speed changes how quickly bits are put on the wire, not how fast light travels through the fibre. Propagation does not scale with bandwidth.

options.text: RTT barely changes: about 50 ms of it is propagation over 5,000 km of fibre, which bandwidth cannot reduce
options.explanation: Correct. At about 1 ms of RTT per 100 km, 5,000 km of route gives roughly 50 ms of unavoidable propagation. The rest is routers, queues and endpoints; serialization of a small ping on a 1 Gbit/s link is already microseconds.

options.text: RTT halves, because half of latency is always bandwidth-related
options.explanation: There is no fixed split. On an uncongested long path, propagation dominates small-packet RTT.

options.text: RTT increases, because faster links use more routers
options.explanation: Upgrading the access link does not add hops to the path.

questions.workedExample:
1. Rule of thumb: light in fibre travels about 204,000 km/s, roughly 1 ms of round-trip time per 100 km of route.
2. 5,000 km of route therefore costs about 50 ms of RTT in propagation alone, whatever the link speed.
3. Bandwidth affects serialization: a ping-sized packet takes microseconds to send at 1 Gbit/s, so ten times faster saves almost nothing.
4. To reduce this latency, shorten the path (serve from nearer, better routing), cut the number of round trips, or reduce queueing; a bandwidth upgrade helps large transfers and congestion, not distance.

questions.prompt: Assume Sydney users’ RTT to a Virginia-only service is dominated by geographic propagation, with negligible queueing and serialization. Which change directly reduces the response path’s propagation distance for locally serviceable requests?

options.text: Upgrading the servers' uplinks from 10 to 100 Gbit/s
options.explanation: A capacity increase can reduce serialization or congestion in other circumstances, but it does not shorten the geographic path specified here.

options.text: Switching to HTTP/3 over QUIC
options.explanation: QUIC can reduce setup exchanges in suitable cases, but it does not shorten the specified physical path. Each remaining exchange still incurs that path’s propagation delay.

options.text: Tuning TCP congestion control on the servers
options.explanation: Congestion control can change queueing delay, but under these assumptions it does not shorten the propagation path.

options.text: Serving Sydney users from a region or CDN edge in Australia
options.explanation: Correct for content or requests that the nearer location can serve locally. Requests that still wait on Virginia retain that remote dependency.

questions.workedExample: Placing serviceable data/work near Sydney shortens the relevant path. A CDN hit can help, while a miss or synchronous origin dependency may still wait for Virginia. Protocol changes can reduce the number of exchanges, and routing or queue improvements can reduce RTT in other scenarios. No fixed local RTT is guaranteed.

lessons.title: GEO, LEO and satellite path geometry
lessons.summary: A four-leg vertical bent-pipe model isolates altitude propagation from a complete service path.
lessons.body:
Satellite Internet trades cables for altitude. How high the satellite orbits decides the minimum latency, which is why geostationary links feel sluggish for interactive use while low-Earth-orbit constellations can compete with terrestrial paths.

## A leg-by-leg propagation model

A satellite link in its simplest "bent pipe" form relays signals: your request goes up to the satellite and down to a ground station, and the reply goes up and down again. That is four legs through space, at almost the vacuum speed of light, so the minimum propagation RTT depends mainly on how high the satellite is.

```formula reference
RTT = (md) / v
where
RTT: the propagation round-trip time, in seconds (s)
m: the number of one-way legs the signal travels: 2 for a direct path (there and back), 4 for a satellite bent pipe (up, down, up, down)
d: the length of each leg, in kilometres (km)
v: the propagation speed: about 204,000 km/s in fibre, about 299,792 km/s in vacuum
In words: the round trip is the number of legs times the length of each, divided by the signal speed; a satellite path has twice as many legs as a direct cable, so altitude counts four times.
```

Taking each leg as the satellite's altitude, directly overhead:

| Path | Legs | Propagation RTT |
|---|---|---|
| GEO, 35,786 km up | 4 | about 477 ms |
| LEO, 550 km up | 4 | about 7.3 ms |
| 5,570 km of fibre | 2 | about 55 ms |

These are idealised minimums for propagation alone, not service RTTs.

## GEO satellites

Geostationary satellites orbit at 35,786 km, above the equator, staying fixed in the sky so a dish can point at one permanently. A suitably spaced small GEO set can view much of the non-polar Earth in an ideal coverage model; elevation constraints, beams, capacity and redundancy determine an actual service.

The cost is latency: a request goes up and down, and so does the reply, four legs of nearly 36,000 km. The minimum is about 477 ms of round-trip time from physics alone, under the idealised minimum four-altitude-leg geometry. Slant range, processing and the terrestrial path increase actual RTT; no fixed deployment RTT is assumed. Fine for television broadcast and bulk downloads; painful for interactive use, gaming and many TCP connections.

## LEO constellations

**Low Earth orbit** satellites orbit much nearer Earth than GEO and move across the sky relative to a ground terminal. For a hypothetical 550 km overhead bent-pipe route, four altitude legs contribute about 7.3 ms of propagation. That is not an end-to-end service RTT or a claim about every current commercial orbit shell.

The trade-offs:

- Coverage and capacity determine constellation size; not every LEO service requires thousands of satellites.
- Terminals need suitable satellite tracking and handover, using electronically steered arrays or other supported antenna designs. Handover performance is deployment-specific.
- Traffic must reach a terrestrial gateway somewhere to connect with ground Internet services. Inter-satellite links can move that ground station farther from the user.
- **Laser inter-satellite links** travel approximately at vacuum light speed. A suitably short space route can beat a longer/slower fibre route in propagation, but orbital geometry, actual routing and processing determine the result.
- Shared capacity, obstructions, atmospheric conditions and available ground gateways affect performance.

| | GEO example | LEO example |
|---|---|---|
| Altitude | 35,786 km | Assumed 550 km |
| Four vertical legs at light speed | about 477 ms | about 7.3 ms |
| Apparent motion | approximately fixed for a ground observer | moves across the sky |
| Coverage design | non-polar geometry, beam and capacity constraints | constellation, tracking and handover constraints |

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Current AS/prefix counts, IXP peaks, cable traffic shares, commercial satellite fleet sizes and universal measured RTTs are omitted because no consistent dated measurement was established for them. Satellite and fibre examples use explicit hypothetical distances; they do not predict a particular provider’s service or routing advantage. No cable, orbital-link or ISP performance experiment was run.

## Key takeaways
- A four-leg vertical bent-pipe model isolates altitude propagation from a complete service path.
- Slant range, routing, tracking, gateways and shared capacity shape an operational satellite service.

## Further reading
- [Starlink — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starlink)
- [ESA: Types of orbits](https://www.esa.int/Enabling_Support/Space_Transportation/Types_of_orbits)

questions.prompt: A rural user on geostationary (GEO) satellite broadband says large downloads are fine but video calls feel laggy and web pages with many small requests are slow. The satellite is about 35,786 km up. What is the main explanation?

options.text: The satellite link has too little bandwidth for video
options.explanation: The user reports large downloads are fine, so capacity is not the main issue. The symptoms affect interactive, round-trip-heavy traffic.

options.text: Each round trip must travel up to the satellite and down twice, about 143,000 km, so propagation alone adds nearly half a second to every RTT
options.explanation: Correct. Four legs of about 36,000 km at the speed of light take about 477 ms, before slant range, processing and ground routing are added. Anything that waits for replies suffers; bulk transfers with large windows are less affected.

options.text: Radio signals travel much slower through space than through fibre
options.explanation: Signals in vacuum travel at the full speed of light, faster than in fibre. The problem is the enormous distance, not the speed.

options.text: Satellite links drop most packets, forcing constant retransmissions
options.explanation: Loss can occur, but the symptoms described (bulk fine, interactive slow) match high latency, which the altitude guarantees.

questions.workedExample:
1. A bent-pipe satellite relays signals: request up and down, reply up and down, four legs in total.
2. At GEO altitude each leg is at least about 35,786 km, so a round trip covers about 143,000 km. At about 300,000 km/s that takes roughly 477 ms.
3. Slant range (you are rarely directly under the satellite), processing and terrestrial backhaul make the real RTT larger still.
4. Interactive traffic and protocols with many round trips (handshakes, chains of small requests) feel every one of those half-seconds; a large download, once flowing with a big enough window, mainly needs capacity.
5. Lower orbits (LEO) cut the propagation component dramatically, which is why LEO constellations target interactive use.

questions.prompt: Over a very long distance, a route that goes up to low Earth orbit, across between satellites by laser, and back down can have lower propagation delay than a submarine fibre route between the same places, even though it travels further. Why?

options.text: Light travels about 47% faster in vacuum than in glass, and the extra distance up and down is small compared with a long intercontinental path
options.explanation: Correct. Fibre slows light to about 204,000 km/s against about 300,000 km/s in vacuum. Two extra legs of a few hundred kilometres matter little over, say, 17,000 km, but they dominate on short routes, where fibre wins.

options.text: Satellites have more bandwidth than fibre
options.explanation: Bandwidth does not set propagation delay. Fibre systems typically carry far more capacity than satellite links.

options.text: Laser links skip routing entirely, so there is no processing delay
options.explanation: Satellites and ground stations still switch and process traffic; the advantage is in propagation speed.

options.text: A space route is always faster than fibre, whatever the distance
options.explanation: On short routes the extra up-and-down legs outweigh the speed advantage, and real orbital geometry, hops and ground routing can erase it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Propagation delay is distance divided by signal speed.
2. In fibre, light travels at about 204,000 km/s; in vacuum, about 300,000 km/s, roughly 47% faster.
3. A hypothetical 17,000 km route: fibre gives a round trip of about 167 ms. Going up 550 km, across 17,000 km and down 550 km (about 6% further) at vacuum speed gives about 121 ms.
4. Over a short route, though, the extra climb and descent dominate and fibre wins.
5. Real constellations add slant range, inter-satellite hop geometry, ground routing and processing, so no actual service advantage is guaranteed by this idealised comparison.
